Quick start

  1. Click anywhere once so the browser allows alarm sound. Check the top bar shows 🔔 Sound on.
  2. The session opens at design: feed 6.8 L/s, outlet 350 °C, burner firing. Open Process & Design → P&ID to see the plant, then Operate → DCS console to operate it.
  3. Go to Exercises, pick a list (Training, Think EQUIPPED, Procedures or Visual plant) and click an exercise to load it. A blue banner gives the situation; click Acknowledge on the banner to hide it.
  4. Operate from the DCS console: click an instrument bubble to open its faceplate on the right, change mode, set point or output there. Go out on Visual plant 3D to read local gauges, look at the flame and work hand valves.
  5. Use Speed to run faster (2×–20×) and Freeze to pause while you think.
  6. When finished, open Debrief and grading for your score, then Data export to download CSV files for your report.

2 · Top bar

ControlWhat it does
ClockSimulated time since the session or exercise started (hh:mm:ss).
Freeze / RunPauses and resumes the simulation. Nothing changes while frozen, but you can still read and click.
Speed1×, 2×, 5×, 10× or 20× real time. Grading uses simulated time, so speed does not change your score.
Status lampGreen: firing, with the control configuration (rev A, ratio or rev B trim). Amber: purging or purged. Red: BMS tripped. Click it to open the BMS screen.
🔔 Sound on / 🔕 Sound offSwitches the audible alarm. One short beep = new alarm; two alternating tones = trip or flame failure. It repeats until acknowledged or silenced.
SilenceStops the sound only. Alarms keep flashing in the list until acknowledged. A new alarm sounds again.
AcknowledgeAcknowledges every alarm in the list (same as Acknowledge all). Unacknowledged alarms older than 60 s cost points.
ScoreContinuous score for this session (starts at 100).

4 · DCS console

Display buttons above the drawing:

  • Overview: all instruments, plus a summary at top left (feed and duty, fuel and air, heat released, stack plume).
  • Temperature profile: temperature instruments only, with a chart of the process path (TI-010 → TI-020 → TI-022 → TT-040) and flue-gas path (TIAH-023 → TI-021). Dashed lines are design.
  • Draft profile: pressures from windbox to stack top, O₂ at firebox and stack, and a chart against the red atmospheric line. A point right of the red line means positive pressure.
  • Fuel system: fuel train instruments with a table of header, valve, gun pressure, fuel flow, shut-off valve states, flame and air : fuel ratio.

Instrument bubbles follow ISA style: letters on top (e.g. TIC = temperature indicating controller), loop number below, live value underneath. Controllers show their mode (MAN, AUTO, CAS) at upper right. A value in red is in alarm; a flashing value is not yet acknowledged. A square around a bubble marks a trip switch (FSLL, TSHH, BSLL).

Clicking: click any bubble, valve HV-400 or HV-063, a pump, HV-221 or the burner label to open its faceplate on the right. With the keyboard, Tab to an item and press Enter.

6 · Trend and alarm summary

  • Trend group: Feed, fuel and outlet temperature; Heater group; Combustion; Temperature profile; or Selected tag (PV, SP and OUT of the faceplate you have open).
  • Window: 5, 10, 30 or 60 min. Colours: classic console pens or high contrast. Each pen has its own range, shown in the legend with the latest value.
  • Alarm summary: newest unacknowledged first. Click a row to acknowledge it and open that instrument. Acknowledge all clears the list of acknowledged, returned alarms.

7 · Burner management (BMS)

Button / panelWhat it does
Sequence barIDLE → PURGING → PURGED → RUN. The current state is highlighted; TRIPPED is shown in red with the first-out cause and a timer for purge or ignition.
Reset BMSClears a trip. Refused while the trip cause is still present.
Start purgeStarts the purge timer when every purge permissive is green. If one is lost, the purge stops and returns to IDLE.

Emergency tripImmediate shutdown of the burner, as a real ESD pushbutton.
Purge permissivesGreen ● = satisfied, red ○ = not yet. All must be green to purge.
Trip conditionsAmber ● = condition present now; ▶ in red = the first-out cause of the last trip.
Fuel train and flameStates of XV-301, XV-302, XV-303, flame scanner, gun pressure, windbox draft and FV-300.
Add FY-005 air/fuel ratioAdds a ratio relay so FIC-005 in Cascade follows fuel flow. The ratio starts at the present air : fuel value and can be changed with Set.
Put rev B in serviceAdds O₂ trim from the firebox analyzer AI-028 on top of the ratio (±20 % on the air set point).

8 · Field and Visual plant 3D

  • Pump cards: start or stop P-100A and P-100B. HV-221: snuffing steam into the firebox (use only when the burner is out or in a fire emergency).
  • Look at the stack: what an outside operator sees (clear, hazy or black plume).
  • Laboratory flue gas sample: a sampled O₂ result arrives 2 simulated minutes later and appears as a banner and in the log.
  • Local gauge check: actual positions of FV-300, FV-200, HV-400 and a description of the flame.

Visual plant 3D

  • Walk: Next ▶ / ◀ Prev follow the outside-operator round (12 stations, yellow arrows on the floor); the pad (▲ ▼ ⟲ ⟳ ⤒ ⤓) or a drag in the picture walks and looks freely. ⌂ Home returns to the muster point.
  • Read and look: the card beside the picture lists each station's items; ◀ Read zooms to a gauge and shows its dial, ◀ Look describes the flame, the stack plume or the equipment. Every reading is written to the event log.
  • Hand valves: ◀ Operate opens the valve panel; Open and Close act on the model at once (a closed suction valve starves the pump, a closed heating-fluid valve cools TI-010). Car-sealed (CSO) and locked (LC) valves refuse.
  • Labels: Tour shows tag and live value; Identify blanks the boxes for the identification exercise; Off clears the picture.
  • Below the picture: identification (check a station, finish and grade), the rounds sheet (28 readings and states, graded against the live plant), gauge locations by level and the hand-valve table.

9 · Exercises

  • Load an exercise: choose the list (Training, Think EQUIPPED, Procedures) and click one. The plant is reset to its starting state; faults appear on their own schedule. The exercise name shows above the drawing.
  • Procedure tracker: each step is ticked with its time when the simulator sees it done (a ! marks a step done out of order); steps the simulator cannot see have a Mark done button. Tick Communicated with the right people when you have, then press Finish and grade (it also grades itself at the time limit).
  • What-if: choose an event, set ↑ / ↓ / = for each variable, then Check my predictions. The model runs a copy offline and marks each answer.
  • Trend matching: Generate four trends draws four unlabelled 10-minute responses (pens: feed, outlet temperature, fuel, CO, firebox temperature, firebox pressure); choose the initiating event for each and check.
  • Scrambles: give each step its position number from the drop-down, then Check order. Wrong steps show their correct position.
  • DCS reading sheet: Start reading sheet, type each value and its alarm limits (leave a limit blank if there is none), then Check sheet.
  • Field checks: every training exercise lists what an outside operator should read or look at on Visual plant 3D; the items tick from the event log and Grade the field check scores it out of 5.
  • Visual plant list: VP-1 to VP-8 (find your way, read the gauges, utilities, a spare pump not lined up, a hand valve left closed, identification, rounds sheet); answer in the panel and press Check and grade (out of 10).
  • Think EQUIPPED cases are worked in the Systematic problem solving tab: the course Woods troubleshooting workbook, on the H-100 unit, pulls the trends, the readings against design and the event log from the simulator as datasets.

10 · Debrief and data export

  • Debrief: continuous score with each deduction, performance indicators (time on target, highest temperatures, CO), exercise grades, fault recovery times, and the event log. Filter the log by type and use Copy log.
  • Data export: tick the data sets, choose range and interval, check the preview, then download. The claude.ai page asks you to confirm each file; on GitHub Pages it downloads directly. Files are UTF-8 CSV; the first three lines starting with # are a header.

Nothing is stored after you close or reload the page. Download your CSV files before leaving.

The process · H-100 natural-draft fired heater

Teaching slide deck (101 slides, interactive) — fundamentals and equations, design, operation, process description, P&ID and control, DCS/HMI, other unit operations, and every exercise with its objective.
Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)
1 Principle of operation · 2 What each unit does · 3 Steady-state operating conditions · 4 Process description

1 · Principle of operation

A fired heater raises the temperature of a process fluid by burning fuel. Here a liquid hydrocarbon feed of 6.8 L/s must reach 350 °C before the packed-bed reactor V-200. The feed is first preheated in E-100 to about 180 °C with heating fluid from Unit A; H-100 supplies the remaining 170 °C — about 2.3 MW.

Where the heat goes

  • Radiant section (firebox): the flame and the hot flue gas (about 1000 °C) radiate to the tubes lining the walls. Radiation grows with the fourth power of absolute temperature, Qrad ∝ (Tgas4 − Ttube4), so this section absorbs about two thirds of the duty.
  • Convection section: the flue gas, now cooler, flows across banks of tubes at the top and gives up heat by convection before it leaves at about 400 °C. The feed passes here first (counter-current), which is why it enters the coil at the top.
  • Losses: the flue gas leaving the stack carries away most of the rest (about 17 %); about 2 % is lost through the casing. Thermal efficiency is about 81 %.

The balances that govern it

BalanceRelationAt design
Process dutyQ = ṁ cp (Tout − Tin)5.44 kg/s × 2.5 kJ/kg K × (350 − 180) K = 2312 kW
Fuel neededṁfuel = Q / (η × LHV)2312 / (0.815 × 42 000) = 0.0676 kg/s = 243 kg/h
Air neededṁair = λ × AFRst × ṁfuel1.11 × 14.4 × 243 = 3892 kg/h (10 % excess air)
Heat release limitQrel = min(ṁfuel LHV, ṁO2 × 13.1 MJ/kg)Fuel-limited at design; becomes air-limited when λ < 1
Flue gas O2O2 (dry) ≈ 21 (1 − 1/λ)λ 1.11 → about 2.1 % in the firebox
Natural draftΔp ≈ g H (ρair − ρflue)Hot light flue gas in the stack pulls about −2.5 mmH2O at the arch and −6 mmH2O at the floor

Why air matters

Fuel only releases heat if there is oxygen to burn it. With about 10 % excess air all the fuel burns and the flame is short and bright. If fuel rises while air does not, the firebox goes fuel-rich (λ < 1): the extra fuel leaves as CO and soot, the flame becomes long and lazy, radiation to the tubes falls, and the outlet temperature drops even though more fuel is being fired. Too much air is safe but wasteful — every extra kilogram of air is heated from 20 °C to 400 °C and thrown away up the stack.

Why draft matters

There is no fan. The column of hot flue gas in the stack is lighter than the outside air, so the pressure inside the heater is slightly below atmospheric. That suction pulls combustion air in through the intake screen F-100, the air valve FV-200 and the burner register, and keeps flue gas from leaking out of the peep doors. The stack damper HV-400 sets how strong the draft is. Close it too far and the firebox pressure goes positive and the burner is starved of air.

3 · Steady-state operating conditions

"Design" is the lined-out steady state the simulator starts from. "Now" updates live from the running simulation so you can compare any upset with the steady state.

Stream table

Equipment performance

4 · Process description

Slide version with interactive simulations: see the teaching deck linked at the top of this tab (Parts 4, 5 and 7 cover this section).

Feed system. Hydrocarbon feed is drawn from TK-101 by P-100A (P-100B is the installed spare) and pumped at about 1030 kPa to the shell-and-tube preheater E-100. Heating fluid from Unit A enters E-100 at 230 °C through the hand valve HV-063 and returns to Unit A; it raises the feed from 40 °C to 180 °C (TI-010). PSV-101 protects the feed side of E-100 against overpressure if it is blocked in while hot fluid flows.

Feed control. The preheated feed passes the flow element shared by FIC-003, FIAL-008 and FSLL-008 and then the flow control valve FV-010. FIC-003 holds 6.8 L/s. FV-010 fails open so the coil is never left without flow by an instrument failure; FSLL-008 trips the burner if flow falls below 3.4 L/s, because a hot coil without flow overheats in seconds.

Heater coil. The feed enters the convection section at the top of H-100 (TI-020, 180 °C) and flows down through the convection tubes, counter-current to the rising flue gas, reaching about 233 °C at the crossover (TI-022). It then passes to the radiant tubes on the firebox walls, where it is heated to 350 °C. It leaves at the bottom (TT-040, TIAH-025, PI-005) and flows to the packed-bed reactor V-200.

Combustion. Fuel oil from the fuel system passes V-121, the flow element FI-001, the safety shut-off valves XV-301 and XV-302 with the bleed XV-303 between them, the control valve FV-300 and V-122 to the burner gun, where it is atomised at about 600 kPa (PIAL-020). Combustion air is drawn in by natural draft through the intake screen F-100 and the air valve FV-200 into the windbox under the burner. The flame fires upward into the firebox; BS-005 watches it.

Flue gas path. Hot flue gas (about 990 °C, TIAH-023) rises through the firebox, passes the convection tubes, and leaves through the breaching and stack at about 400 °C (TI-021). The stack damper HV-400 sets the draft; firebox pressure is about −2.5 mmH2O at the arch (PI-003) and −6 mmH2O at the floor (PI-004). Oxygen is measured in the firebox (AI-028, about 2.1 %) and at the stack exit (AI-029, about 3.2 %, higher because air leaks into the convection section), and CO at the stack exit (AI-026).

Control philosophy. TIC-030 controls the outlet temperature by moving the fuel valve FV-300 only. FIC-005 controls combustion air on its own set point (P&ID rev A); the operator must raise air before raising firing and lower fuel before lowering air. Two optional upgrades can be tested: FY-005 ratio (air follows fuel) and rev B O2 trim from AI-028.

Safety systems. The burner management system requires a timed purge of the firebox with draft air before light-off, lights the burner at low fire with a 10 s trial for ignition, and trips the fuel on low feed flow (FSLL-008), high outlet temperature (TSHH-025), low fuel pressure at the gun (PSLL-020), loss of windbox draft (PSLL-030), flame failure (BSLL-005) or the emergency pushbutton. A trip closes XV-301 and XV-302, opens XV-303, closes FV-300 and opens FV-200 and HV-400 to purge the box.

Operating envelope. Normal: outlet 350 ± 1 °C, firebox O2 1.5–4 %, CO below 100 ppm, firebox pressure negative, tube skin below 430 °C, FV-300 and FV-200 between 20 and 85 % open so both loops keep control margin. The feed rate can be raised to about 8.2 L/s only if air is raised first (to about 4800 kg/h).

How a heater like H-100 is specified and roughed out before detailed design. Numbers are for the H-100 design case (6.8 L/s feed, 180 → 350 °C). The sizing in section 5 is conceptual: it uses rules of thumb and simple correlations, not a vendor thermal rating.

1 Fundamentals and principle · 2 Components · 3 Setting the operating conditions · 4 Conceptual design · 5 Conceptual sizing (calculator)

1 · Fundamentals and principle of the unit operation

A fired heater is a direct-fired heat exchanger: fuel burns in an open firebox and the heat passes through the walls of tubes to a process fluid flowing inside them. It is used when the required temperature is above what steam or hot oil can supply, or when the duty is too large for them. Four pieces of physics decide how it behaves.

1.1 Energy balance: the duty

The process fluid must absorb Q = ṁ cp (Tout − Tin). For H-100: 5.44 kg/s × 2.5 kJ/kg K × 170 K = 2312 kW absorbed. The fuel must supply more than this, because some heat leaves with the flue gas and through the casing:

Qfired = Q / η    η = 1 − (stack loss) − (casing loss)

Stack loss = (kg flue gas per kg fuel) × cp,flue × (Tstack − Tamb) / LHV. At 400 °C stack and 11 % excess air this is about 16.6 %; with 2 % casing loss η ≈ 81.5 % and Qfired ≈ 2840 kW. Stack temperature and excess air are the two things that set efficiency.

1.2 Combustion

  • Fuel oil (≈ CH1.8) needs about 14.4 kg air per kg fuel for complete combustion (stoichiometric air : fuel ratio AFRst). Its lower heating value is about 42 MJ/kg.
  • The air ratio λ = actual air / stoichiometric air. Excess air = (λ − 1) × 100 %. Dry flue gas O2 ≈ 21 (1 − 1/λ) %, which is why O2 is the operator's measure of excess air.
  • Heat can only be released if oxygen is available: Qrel = min(ṁfuel LHV, ṁO2 × 13.1 MJ per kg O2). Below λ = 1 extra fuel produces CO and soot, not heat.
  • Oil burners in natural draft need roughly 10–25 % excess air (O2 ≈ 2–4 %) to burn cleanly; more than that wastes fuel heating air that goes up the stack.

1.3 Heat transfer: radiant section

In the firebox the flame and the hot, emitting gases (CO2, H2O) radiate to the tubes. A simplified form of the Lobo–Evans method is

Qr = σ αAcp F (Tg4 − Tt4) + hc At (Tg − Tt)

where σ is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, αAcp the effective cold-plane area of the tube row, F an exchange factor from gas emissivity and geometry, Tg the gas (bridgewall) temperature and Tt the tube wall temperature, both absolute. Because of the fourth power, the radiant section takes most of the duty (about 69 % in H-100) even though it has about the same tube area as the convection section. The simulator uses Qr = Kr(Tg4 − Tt4).

Designers work with the average radiant heat flux q″ = Qr / Ar (kW per m² of outside tube area). Typical values for liquid hydrocarbon service are about 25–40 kW/m². The flux is not uniform: the side of a wall tube that faces the flame receives about 1.8 times the average (single row, 2 × OD pitch), so the peak flux sets the hottest tube metal.

1.4 Heat transfer: convection section

Above the firebox the gas is too cool to radiate strongly and heat is transferred by forced convection across tube banks: Qc = U A ΔTLM, or in effectiveness form ε = 1 − e−NTU when the flue gas is the minimum-capacity stream. Gas-side coefficients are low (about 20–40 W/m² K on bare tubes), so convection tubes are usually studded or finned after the first two rows. The first two rows, called shield tubes, are bare because they also see radiation from the firebox.

1.5 Tube wall temperature

Heat flowing into a tube raises the metal above the fluid: Tskin ≈ Tfluid + q″(do/di)(1/hi + Rcoke) + q″ do ln(do/di)/(2kw). High flux, low velocity (low hi) or coke inside the tube all raise the skin temperature. This limit, not the flame, usually decides how hard a heater can be fired.

1.6 Natural draft

A column of hot flue gas is lighter than the same column of outside air, so the pressure inside the heater is below atmospheric: Δp = g H (ρair − ρflue). In mmH2O this is simply H [m] × Δρ [kg/m³]. The stack and the firebox itself both generate draft; the burner, convection bank, damper and stack friction consume it. The design target is a small negative pressure (about −2 to −3 mmH2O) at the arch, the highest-pressure point in the radiant box, so flue gas never leaks out.

Order in which the conditions are set

  1. Flow first: establish feed flow (FIC-003) before firing and never fire without it; the fluid is the tube coolant.
  2. Draft next: set HV-400 so the arch is about −2.5 mmH2O at the present firing.
  3. Air before fuel: when increasing firing raise air first; when decreasing cut fuel first (lead–lag). Air follows fuel only after FY-005 is added.
  4. Outlet temperature: TIC-030 in AUTO trims fuel to hold 350 °C.
  5. Optimise: reduce air until firebox O2 is about 2 % with CO below 100 ppm; re-check draft (air and draft interact).
  6. Check limits: tube skin, bridgewall and stack temperatures inside their alarms.

Operating window

Minimum: the burner turndown (about 3 : 1 for an oil burner) and FSLL-008 at 3.4 L/s. Maximum: the natural draft available to pull air through the burner, FV-200 capacity (about 6000 kg/h range), and the tube skin alarm. Example: 8.2 L/s at 350 °C needs about 2790 kW absorbed, ≈ 295 kg/h fuel and ≈ 4700–4800 kg/h air. Press Size for 8.2 L/s in section 5: the fuel and air rows give the requirement; the geometry rows show the heater you would design for that rate (compare with H-100 to see what is short).

4.3 Design sequence

  1. Heat and material balance: duty, fuel, air, flue gas (section 5 steps 1–3).
  2. Choose excess air and stack temperature → efficiency → fired duty.
  3. Split duty between radiant and convection (radiant 60–75 % typical); find bridgewall temperature.
  4. Radiant section: choose average flux → area → tube size, pitch, number and length → firebox diameter and height; check H/D, velocity and tube skin.
  5. Convection section: LMTD and U → area → rows of bare shield tubes and studded tubes.
  6. Draft: firebox and stack draft balance → stack height and diameter.
  7. Burner selection and clearances, hydraulics (coil pressure drop), materials, instruments and BMS.
  8. Hand the data sheet to the vendor for rating (API 560 data sheet).

Assumptions and limits of this sizing

  • Flue gas cp is taken constant; bridgewall temperature comes from an energy balance on the radiant box, not from a radiation model.
  • The radiant/convection split is an input (typical 60–75 %); in a real design it results from the Lobo–Evans calculation.
  • Inside coefficient: Dittus–Boelter, Nu = 0.023 Re0.8 Pr0.4, with the viscosity and conductivity entered; no fouling. Peak flux = factor × average (≈ 1.8 for one row at 2 × OD pitch against the wall).
  • Firebox inside diameter = tube circle + 3 × OD. Convection tube length = tube-circle diameter.
  • Draft: ideal-gas densities at 1 atm; the firebox draft gain uses the bridgewall temperature over the radiant height.
  • Guidelines quoted (H/D, flux, velocity, stack velocity) are typical design practice, e.g. API 560, and are not a substitute for a vendor rating.

HAZID · Hazard Identification of the H-100 plant

A plant-level, checklist-driven identification of the major hazards around the heater, done before (and wider than) the detailed HAZOP. It uses the same example risk matrix as the HAZOP tab; a real study uses the owner's matrix and a multidisciplinary team.

Teaching slide deck · HAZID (24 slides, interactive) — what HAZID is, the PFD areas, guideword checklist, bow-tie and risk matrix, major hazards and follow-up studies.

1 What HAZID is · 2 Method · 3 PFD and study areas · 4 Guideword checklist · 5 Hazard register · 6 Major accident hazards · 7 From HAZID to HAZOP

1 · What HAZID is and where it sits

HAZID (Hazard Identification) is a structured brainstorming of what could go badly wrong across the whole facility, including its surroundings, people and environment. It is done early (concept and front-end design) with the PFD, layout and design basis, so that major hazards shape the design before details are fixed. It asks broad questions ("what hazards exist here?"), where HAZOP asks detailed ones ("what if the flow in this line is less than intended?").

HAZIDHAZOP
WhenConcept / FEED, and before major changesDetailed design, P&ID frozen; revalidation
DrawingPFD, plot planP&ID, cause-and-effect chart
BreakdownAreas / systemsNodes with one design intent
PromptGuideword checklist by hazard category (natural, external, process, utilities, health, occupational, environment, operations)Guide word × parameter (NO flow, MORE temperature …)
ScopeProcess and non-process hazards, site and surroundingsProcess deviations and operability
OutputHazard register, list of major accident hazards, studies to do next (HAZOP, fire and explosion, QRA, SIL, layout)Worksheets and recommendations per deviation
ReferenceISO 17776 (major accident hazard management in design; HAZID and its checklist); company HSE practiceIEC 61882

2 · Method

  1. Define scope and basis: H-100 with feed tank, pumps, E-100, fuel and air systems, stack, outlet to V-200; site conditions; risk matrix.
  2. Divide the plant into areas on the PFD (section 3).
  3. Apply the guideword checklist to each area (section 4): for every category ask whether the hazard exists here, what could release it (cause / threat) and what would follow (top event and outcome).
  4. Record existing controls, split into prevention (stops the top event) and mitigation (limits the outcome), as in a bow-tie.
  5. Rank the risk (S × L with the controls) and flag major accident hazards (MAH): events that could cause multiple fatalities, major damage or a major environmental release.
  6. Assign actions and further studies: design changes, HAZOP nodes, fire and explosion analysis, SIL assessment, layout review.

6 · Major accident hazards and what they lead to

    7 · From HAZID to HAZOP and other studies

    • Every process MAH is examined in detail in the HAZOP (tab HAZOP): firebox explosion → nodes N7 and N9; tube rupture → N4; fuel leak → N5; fuel-rich firing → N5, N6, N7.
    • Trips that protect against MAHs (BMS purge and flame supervision, FSLL-008, TSHH-025) go to a SIL assessment (IEC 61511).
    • Fire hazards (HZ-03, HZ-04, HZ-05, HZ-14, HZ-16) go to a fire and explosion analysis and a layout / separation-distance check.
    • Occupational and health hazards (HZ-17 to HZ-22) go to the permit-to-work, confined-space and PPE procedures.
    • The HAZID register is revisited when the design changes (management of change).

    4 · Degrees of freedom (DOF)

    Why it matters. The degrees of freedom tell the designer how many variables can be controlled independently. If you try to control more CVs than there are independent MVs, controllers fight over one valve; if you control fewer, some variable drifts wherever the disturbances push it.

    NDOF = Nvariables − Nindependent equations    and    NDOF = Ndisturbances (fixed by surroundings) + Nmanipulated

    For control, the useful count is the control DOF = number of independent manipulated variables, which for a process unit is usually the number of independent control valves (and dampers, speeds).

    4.1 DOF of H-100 (steady state)

    Variables (13)Equations (8)
    F feed flow · Tin · Tout · W fuel · A air · λ · Tg firebox · Ts stack · Q duty · O₂ · Parch draft · d damper position · h HV-063 position 1 E-100: Tin = f(F, h, Thot)
    2 Duty: Q = F ρ cp(Tout − Tin)
    3 Firebox energy balance: heat released = f(W, A) → Tg
    4 Radiant + convection transfer: Q = f(Tg, Tin, Tout)
    5 Flue-gas balance → Ts
    6 λ = A / (AFRst W)
    7 O₂ = 21(1 − 1/λ)
    8 Draft: Parch = f(d, Ts, A + W)

    DOF = 13 − 8 = 5. Parameters such as Thot, ambient temperature and LHV are disturbances, not counted. The five DOF match exactly the five independent handles: FV-010, FV-300, FV-200, HV-400, HV-063. So at most five variables can be held at chosen values. The design picks them by the objectives in section 1:

    4.2 DOF of each loop

    • A feedback loop uses one DOF: it turns "valve position is free" into "CV = SP". The SP becomes the new free input, now given by the operator (or a higher controller).
    • Cascade and ratio do not create DOF. FY-005 and AIC-027 all act through the one valve FV-200: ratio fixes A/W, the trim adjusts that ratio to hold O₂. Still one DOF, used better.
    • A controller in MAN gives its DOF back to the operator (loop open). A valve at 0 % or 100 % (saturated) loses its DOF: the CV is then uncontrolled. Example: when FV-200 is wide open and more fuel is needed, O₂ can no longer be held.
    • Two controllers must never move the same valve at the same time (unless a selector or split range decides which one acts).

    5 · The control loops on the P&ID

    6 · How the loops were chosen for this P&ID (หลักการกำหนด control loop)

    1. Start from the objectives and the DOF. Five handles, so at most five fixed variables; the ranking in section 1 decides which ones get automatic control (quality, throughput, combustion) and which are left to the operator (draft, preheat).
    2. Pair each CV with the MV that affects it most directly, fastest and with one sign. Fuel → outlet temperature: gain about 2.8 °C per % of valve, response time constant about 105 s, dead time about 8 s (from the step test in section 8.4). Air also moves the outlet temperature, but its effect changes sign at λ = 1 (more air cools an air-rich box, heats a fuel-rich one), so air cannot be the handle for temperature.
    3. Put fast flow loops on the valves (FIC-003, FIC-005). A flow loop removes valve non-linearity and upstream pressure changes within seconds, so the slower outer loop sees a clean handle.
    4. Keep safety separate from control. TSHH-025 uses its own element (TIAH-025), not TT-040; FSLL-008 is separate from FIC-003. A failed control transmitter must not disable its own trip.
    5. Choose fail positions for the safe state, independent of controller action: fuel FC, feed FO (coolant keeps flowing), air FO and damper FO (keep air and draft).
    6. Protect against the dangerous direction. Rev A leaves air on its own SP, so fuel increases can make the box fuel-rich. The fix is structural: ratio FY-005 makes air follow fuel, O₂ trim corrects the ratio, and cross-limiting (proposed, section 7) makes air lead on increases and fuel lead on decreases.
    7. Avoid interacting loops. Draft and air flow both depend on the damper and the burner register. Automatic draft control on HV-400 would fight FIC-005, so draft is set by hand and checked after firing changes.
    8. Measure what matters where it matters. O₂ in the firebox (AI-028) is used for trim, not the stack O₂ (AI-029), which also sees tramp air leaking into the convection section.
    9. Leave slow, rarely changed handles in manual (HV-063, HV-400), with alarms (TI-010 LO, PI-003 HI) to call the operator.
    Pairing testFuel → ToutAir → ToutAir → O₂Damper → draft
    Direct effectyesindirect (via combustion)yesyes
    Sign constant over operating rangeyes (while air-rich)no, flips at λ = 1yesyes
    Speedτ ≈ 105 s—τ ≈ 11 sseconds
    DecisionTIC-030not usedAIC-027 (rev B)manual, avoids interaction

    7 · Loop structures: the principle of each (หลักการพื้นฐานของ control loop แต่ละแบบ)

    StructurePrincipleUse it whenOn H-100
    Manual (open loop)The operator sets the valve; nothing corrects disturbances.The variable changes rarely or an auto loop would interact.HIC-400 damper, HIC-063 preheat
    Single feedbackMeasure CV, compare with SP, move MV to remove the error. Corrects any disturbance, but only after it has moved the CV.Almost always the base layer.FIC-003, FIC-005, TIC-030
    CascadeThe outer (master) controller sets the SP of an inner (slave) controller on a faster variable. The inner loop removes its own disturbances before they reach the outer CV. Inner loop must be 3–5 times faster.A fast disturbance acts on the MV path (e.g. fuel pressure).Proposed: TIC-030 → fuel flow FIC → FV-300. FIC-005 in CAS is the inner loop of FY-005.
    RatioOne flow's SP = ratio × another (wild) flow. Keeps a proportion without waiting for a quality measurement.Blending, air : fuel.FY-005: air SP = R × fuel (R ≈ 16 kg/kg at design)
    Feedback trim on a ratioA slow analyzer controller adjusts the ratio to correct what the ratio cannot know (fuel quality, meter error, leakage).Composition measurement available but slow.AIC-027 (AI-028 O₂) trims FY-005 by ±20 % (rev B)
    FeedforwardMeasure a disturbance and move the MV before the CV changes, using a model of its effect. Needs feedback to remove model error.A large, measurable disturbance.Proposed: feed flow × (TSP − Tin) → fuel demand, added to TIC-030 output
    Cross-limiting (lead–lag)Two selectors: fuel SP ≤ what the measured air can burn; air SP ≥ what the measured fuel needs. Air leads on increase, fuel leads on decrease; the box never goes fuel-rich.Combustion control of boilers and heaters.Proposed upgrade beyond rev B
    Override / selectorTwo controllers share one valve through a low or high selector; the one nearest its limit takes over.Protect a constraint (tube skin, fuel pressure) while normally controlling another CV.Possible: tube-skin TIC overriding TIC-030 on the fuel valve
    Split rangeOne controller output drives two valves in sequence (0–50 % valve A, 50–100 % valve B).One CV needs two handles (heat and cool).Not used on H-100
    Safety interlock (BMS / SIS)Discrete logic on independent sensors: if a limit is crossed, drive to the safe state. Not a control loop and not bypassed by the operator.Hazards that control cannot be trusted with.FSLL-008, TSHH-025, PSLL-020, PSLL-030, BSLL-005, ESD

    8 · Control modes: P, PI and PID (แนวทางการควบคุม P, PI, PID)

    The simulator uses the ideal PID form, with signals in % of span, derivative on the measurement and anti-windup clamp:

    OUT(t) = Kc [ e(t) + (1/Ti) ∫e dt − Td dPV/dt ] + bias

    8.1 What each term does

    ModeActionGoodBadTypical use
    P (proportional)OUT change ∝ error now.Simple, immediate, stable at low gain.Offset: after a load change the error settles at e = Δload / (1 + KcK), not zero. High gain → oscillation.Averaging level control, where offset does not matter.
    PI (+ integral)Adds the accumulated error; keeps moving OUT until the error is zero.No offset. The industrial default (most loops).Slower, more overshoot if Ti is short; windup when the valve saturates (needs anti-windup).Flow, pressure, most temperature and analyzer loops.
    PID (+ derivative)Adds action ∝ rate of change of PV; anticipates.Faster, less overshoot on slow lag-dominated loops with little noise.Amplifies noise; derivative on error kicks on SP changes (use derivative on PV).Slow temperature loops with clean signals; rarely on flow.

    8.2 Guidelines by loop type

    Loop typeModeGainResetDerivative
    Liquid / gas flow (FIC-003, FIC-005)PIlow (0.2–0.8)fast (2–10 s)none (noisy)
    Heater outlet temperature (TIC-030)PI or PIDmoderateabout the process time constantsmall, optional
    O₂ trim (AIC-027)PI, slowlowlong (tens of s to minutes)none
    Level (averaging)P or PIlowlongnone
    Pressure (gas)PIhighfastnone

    8.3 Tuning from a step test (FOPDT model)

    Put the loop in MAN, step OUT, record PV. Fit a first-order-plus-dead-time model G(s) = K e−θs/(τs + 1): K = ΔPV/ΔOUT (both in % of span); from the times to 28.3 % and 63.2 % of the final change, τ = 1.5 (t63 − t28), θ = t63 − τ. Then the lambda (IMC) PI rule with closed-loop time constant λ:

    Kc = τ / [K(λ + θ)],   Ti = τ    (λ = τ for a smooth loop, smaller for a tighter one)

    8.4 H-100 step tests (run on the simulator model) and suggested tuning

    Step tests are computed on a copy of the model when this tab opens; they do not disturb the running session.

    9 · Tuning lab (runs the H-100 model)

    Choose a loop and a test, set the mode and tuning, then Run. The test runs on a copy of the H-100 model from design conditions (30 simulated minutes, noise off); the dashed line is the simulator's own tuning for comparison. The running session is not affected. To use a tuning in the live session, enter it in the loop's faceplate on the DCS console.

    Loop and test
    Controller
    Presets

    Things to try

    1. TIC-030, load disturbance: compare P only with PI. P leaves an offset below 350 °C; the integral term removes it.
    2. TIC-030, SP step: shorten Ti from 60 to 30 s, then 15 s. Overshoot grows (about 0.2 → 0.9 → 1.8 °C). The lambda PI preset gives no overshoot but settles more slowly; Kc = 1.5 with Ti = 60 s is faster still. Tuning is a trade-off, not a single right answer.
    3. TIC-030: add Td = 4 s (PID). Little changes: dead time is small compared with the time constant, so derivative has little to anticipate.
    4. FIC-005, SP step: raise Kc to 2 with Ti = 1 s. The air flow overshoots by about 40 % of the step and the valve swings widely; flow loops want moderate gain and a reset near the process time constant.

    HAZOP · Hazard and Operability Study of H-100

    Teaching slide deck · HAZOP (24 slides, interactive) — IEC 61882 phases, nodes and guide words, a worked worksheet row, safeguards, dynamic check and LOPA.
    Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)
    HAZOP report (PDF) · NDFH-V1-SA-HZP-001 rev A — the study on this tab written up as a project report: cover and revision record, close-out executive summary, report (scope, methodology, sessions, nodes, findings), Appendix 1 worksheets node by node, Appendix 2 study documents (node map, P&ID) and Appendix 3 one action close-out sheet per recommendation, ready for the action parties to fill in.
    Open the HAZOP report (PDF)

    A teaching HAZOP of the heater as drawn on the P&ID tab, done node by node with the IEC 61882 guide words. Risk ranking uses the example matrix below; a real study uses the owner's corporate matrix, a multidisciplinary team and the as-built documents.

    1 Standard and method · 2 Team and documents · 3 Nodes · 4 Guide words and parameters · 5 Risk matrix · 6 Worksheets · 7 Coverage check · 8 Recommendations · 9 Dynamic check on the simulator · 10 Follow-up and close-out

    1 · Standard and method (IEC 61882)

    HAZOP is a structured, team-based examination of a defined system. Each part of the design is compared with its design intent; guide words combined with process parameters generate deviations; for each credible deviation the team records causes, consequences, existing safeguards and, where the risk is not acceptable, recommendations. It finds both hazards (harm to people, environment, assets) and operability problems (the plant cannot make product or be run as intended).

    ReferenceWhat it contributes
    IEC 61882:2016 Hazard and operability studies (HAZOP studies) – Application guideDefinitions, the four phases (definition, preparation, examination, documentation and follow-up), guide words, team roles, recording
    CCPS Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation Procedures (3rd ed.)Practical worksheet format, node selection, "consequence without safeguards", risk ranking, links to LOPA
    IEC 61511 (functional safety, SIS)How HAZOP scenarios feed LOPA and SIL targets for trips such as TSHH-025 or a proposed firebox-pressure trip
    ISO 31000 / owner's risk matrixRisk criteria used to decide whether safeguards are adequate
    API 560, API 556, NFPA 85/86Fired-heater design, instrumentation, burner management and purge practice used as the basis for safeguards
    Thailand: Department of Industrial Works regulation on hazard identification, risk assessment and risk-management plans (B.E. 2543)Legal requirement to identify hazards (HAZOP is an accepted method) and to prepare risk-management plans for factories
    OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119 (PSM), where applicableProcess hazard analysis for covered processes, revalidated at least every five years

    The four phases

    1. Definition: scope (H-100 from TK-101 to the V-200 inlet, fuel and air systems, stack, BMS; excluding V-200 and Unit A), objectives, team, risk matrix.
    2. Preparation: collect the P&ID, PFD, heat and material balance, cause-and-effect (trip) chart, operating procedures, alarm list, datasheets; divide the plant into nodes; write each node's design intent; choose parameters and guide words.
    3. Examination: for each node → state the design intent → choose a parameter → apply each guide word → is the deviation meaningful? → causes → consequences assuming the safeguards fail → existing safeguards → rank the risk → recommend → next guide word. Record all meaningful deviations, including those with adequate safeguards ("full recording"), so the reasoning can be audited.
    4. Documentation and follow-up: worksheets, recommendation register with owners and dates, action close-out, and revalidation after changes (MOC) or periodically.

    2 · Team and documents

    RoleResponsibility
    HAZOP leader (chair)Independent of the design; runs the method, keeps the team on the node, decides when a deviation is covered
    Scribe (recorder)Writes the worksheet live, reads back recommendations
    Process engineer (designer)Explains the design intent, balances and limits
    Operations representativeHow the heater is really run: start-up, upsets, rounds, procedures
    Instrument / control engineerLoops, fail positions, BMS logic, trip independence
    Safety / risk engineerRisk matrix, LOPA follow-up, regulations
    Specialists as neededCombustion / burner vendor, mechanical (tubes, refractory), maintenance

    Documents for this study: P&ID tab (rev A with the rev B upgrades), Process tab (stream table and duties), Design tab (limits and sizing), Control loop design tab, Workbook tab (alarms and trips), start-up and shutdown procedures in the Exercises tab.

    3 · Nodes

    A node is a section of the plant with one clear design intent. Boundaries are put where the intent changes (a pump raises pressure, an exchanger heats, a valve controls, a firebox burns). Procedures get their own node because start-up and shutdown create deviations that steady operation does not.

    4 · Guide words and parameters

    Parameters used: flow, pressure, temperature (process and tube metal), level, composition, heat transfer, flame, integrity (containment), measurement, control, utility, safety system, maintenance, and for procedures: purge, light-off, sequence, relight, shutdown. A deviation is only recorded if it is physically meaningful ("REVERSE temperature" is not).

    5 · Risk matrix (example for teaching)

    Numbers in brackets: how many deviations of this study fall in the cell. Risk = S × L.

    SSeverity (worst credible consequence)
    1First aid; minor damage; no release
    2Medical treatment; short outage; small contained release
    3Lost-time injury; heater shutdown for days; local release
    4Permanent disability or single fatality; major heater damage; fire
    5Multiple fatalities; firebox explosion; fire spreading beyond the unit
    LLikelihood with existing safeguards
    1Remote: not expected in the life of the plant (< 10⁻⁴ /y)
    2Unlikely: known in industry (10⁻⁴–10⁻³ /y)
    3Possible: could happen in the plant life (10⁻³–10⁻² /y)
    4Likely: several times in the plant life (10⁻²–10⁻¹ /y)
    5Frequent: yearly or more

    1–4 Low acceptable · 5–9 Medium reduce if practicable (ALARP), review safeguards · 10–16 High recommendation required, consider LOPA · 20–25 Very high not acceptable, act before operation

    6 · HAZOP worksheets (node by node)

    Consequences are written assuming the safeguards fail (worst credible case). S ranks that consequence; L ranks its likelihood with the listed safeguards working as designed.

    7 · Coverage check: guide words applied in each node

    A dot means that guide word gave no meaningful deviation for any parameter in the node (it was still considered). EARLY / LATE / BEFORE / AFTER apply mainly to the procedure node N9.

    8 · Recommendation register

    9 · Dynamic check of selected deviations on the simulator

    A conventional HAZOP judges consequences qualitatively. Here selected deviations are run on a copy of the H-100 model from design conditions with the existing safeguards active (alarms, BMS trips, controllers in their normal modes, no operator action) for up to 30 min. The result shows whether the safeguards act before harm and how much time the operator has.

    Runs when this tab is opened.

    What the runs tell the HAZOP team

    • N1 loss of feed: FSLL-008 trips within seconds, but the tube skin passes its 430 °C alarm first. The trip works; the margin is short, so the spare-pump auto-start (R01) matters.
    • N6 air meter reading high: no trip at all. O₂ goes to zero, CO rises to thousands of ppm and the outlet temperature falls. Only alarms and the operator protect, which is why R07, R08 and R22 were raised.
    • N5 fuel valve failing high with air unchanged: the outlet temperature falls, because the box goes fuel-rich. "More fuel" is a combustion hazard before it is an over-temperature hazard.
    • N8 damper stuck nearly closed: the firebox goes positive while the windbox draft stays above the PSLL-030 trip point. Nothing trips (R17, R18).
    • N4 outlet transmitter reading low: the real outlet reaches about 367 °C; TIAH-025 alarms but stays below the TSHH-025 trip (R24).

    10 · Follow-up and close-out

    • Each recommendation gets an owner and due date; the owner answers with accepted and done, accepted with alternative (with justification) or rejected (with justification agreed by the HAZOP leader and plant manager).
    • High and very-high scenarios whose protection relies on instrumented trips go to LOPA to set the required SIL (IEC 61511).
    • Any change (e.g. putting rev B in service, adding cross-limiting) goes through management of change, which checks whether the HAZOP must be updated.
    • Revalidate the HAZOP periodically (typically every five years) and after incidents.
    • Use the simulator to train operators on the scenarios the HAZOP found; verify that procedures and alarm responses work.

    Safety layers · layers of protection for H-100

    Teaching slide deck · Safety layers (30 slides, interactive) — the six layers, what each adds to the H-100 P&ID, the operating window, SIS voting and relief-valve rules.
    Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

    Safety must cover failures of equipment (including control) and of people, and more than one failure at a time. The response should be limited, keeping production where possible. So protection is built in layers, each independent of the others, with more strength held in reserve as the event gets more serious. Source: course 2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement · Process Safety, applied to H-100. Set points are taken from the model; values marked "assumed" are for teaching.

    1 The six layers · 2 P&ID layer by layer · 3 What each layer does · 4 Integrity operating window · 5 Independence check · 6 Good practices · 7 Standards

    1 · The six layers

    LayerJobAutomatic?Needs power / computer?Needs a person?
    1 BPCSClosed-loop control keeps the process in its operating regionYesYesSupervises
    2 AlarmsBring an unusual situation to the attention of a personNo actionYesYes: decides
    3 SISStop part of the process (fuel off)YesYes, but de-energise to tripNo (reset only)
    4 ReliefPrevent excessive pressure; divert material safelyYes, self-actuatingNoNo
    5 ContainmentKeep released material from workers, community, environmentPassive or remoteMostly noPartly
    6 Emergency responseEvacuation, fire fighting, health careNoPartlyYes

    Layers 1–4 are the four independent protection layers of the automation. Layers 1–3 all need electrical power, computing and communication, so a power or computer failure could take out all three at once. That is why SIS valves go to their fail position with no power, and why relief, containment and emergency response are kept in reserve. Click a ring to open that layer on the P&ID.

    Start from the bare process (step 0) and add one layer at a time. Each layer draws the instruments and devices it adds in its own colour: green BPCS, gold alarms (the letters of an existing bubble turn gold when an alarm is configured on it, with the limit written beside it), orange SIS, red relief, purple containment, blue emergency response. Items drawn dashed are recommended additions that are not on P&ID-001 rev C.

    6 · Good practices in control for safety, checked on H-100

    #Good practiceH-100
    1Never bypass the SIS logic (never turn it off)No bypass switch on SIS-100; any maintenance override needs a permit, a time limit and a compensating measure.
    2Never mechanically block a control or SIS valve so it cannot closeXV-301/302 have no hand jacks; keep a car-seal register.
    3Never open manual bypasses around control and shutdown valvesThe fuel train has no bypass around FV-300 or XV-301/302: keep it that way.

    The HAZOP tab says what can go wrong; this tab asks how often, and whether the safeguards are reliable enough. It follows the course lectures Reliability for Safety and Process Safety Management and Risk Analysis: generic failure rates, PFD and reliability block diagrams, the LOPA equation with a risk reduction factor, and the bow-tie. Failure data are the course's generic values; frequencies marked "assumed" are for teaching, not for design.

    A1 Definitions · A2 Failure rate · A3 R(t), PFD, proof testing · A4 Block diagrams · A5 Failure data · B1 LOPA method · B2 Criteria · B3 IPLs · B4 H-100 worksheet · B5 Register · C Bow-tie · Standards

    Part A · Reliability for safety

    A1 · Definitions

    TermMeaningOn H-100
    HazardInherent physical or chemical characteristic that can harm people, environment or property (CCPS)Hot hydrocarbon in a fired coil; fuel oil and air in a hot box
    Hazardous eventRelease of material or energy that can cause harmTube rupture; firebox explosion
    RiskRisk = consequence × frequencyA fatality (S5) that is tolerable only below 10−4 /yr
    Tolerable / residual riskRisk accepted in context / risk left after protectionThe LOPA target frequency / the mitigated frequency
    Reliability R(t)Probability of success during an interval of timeFSLL-008 working through a one-year test interval
    PFDProbability of failure on demand; F(t) = 1 − R(t)The chance the trip does not act when flow is lost
    Deterministic / probabilistic analysisCan the design keep events within limits / what is the numerical risk and is it tolerablePSV sized for the worst case / LOPA below

    Is 99.9 % reliability good enough? For a 1-in-1000 failure a year it would mean an unsafe landing every day at a big airport. Safety needs both plant reliability (business continuity) and safety reliability (hazard prevention and mitigation).

    A2 · Failure rate from a population

    λ = ΔNf / (Ns · Δt): failures in the interval divided by the survivors and the interval length. 100 identical units are drawn from a Weibull life model, R(t) = e−(t/α)β; β < 1 is burn-in, β = 1 the useful life (constant λ = 1/α, the exponential model), β > 1 wear-out.



    A3 · R(t), PFD and proof testing

    With a constant failure rate R(t) = e−λt and PFD(t) = F(t) = 1 − e−λt ≈ λt when PFD ≪ 0.1. A standby safeguard fails unseen, so its PFD grows until the next proof test restores it: PFDavg = (1/T)∫0Tλt dt = λT/2. MTTF = ∫R dt = 1/λ.


    SIL (IEC 61511, demand mode)PFDavgRRF
    SIL 110−2 – 10−110 – 100
    SIL 210−3 – 10−2100 – 1 000
    SIL 310−4 – 10−31 000 – 10 000

    A4 · Reliability block diagrams

    ConfigurationPFDReliabilityFailure rate / MTTFPFDavg over test interval T
    Series (multi-component): any failure fails the pathPFDA + PFDBR1·R2λ = λ1 + λ2; MTTF = 1/(λ1+λ2)λT/2 (1oo1); λT (2oo2)
    Parallel (redundancy): all paths must failPFDA × PFDBR1+R2−R1R2MTTF = 1/λ1+1/λ2−1/(λ1+λ2)(λT)²/3 (1oo2)
    2-out-of-3 (complex system)PFDAPFDB+PFDBPFDC+PFDCPFDA——(λT)²

    SIF calculator. A safety instrumented function is sensor → logic solver → final element in series; each subsystem can be redundant. Pick an H-100 trip, change the voting, the SIS-grade failure rates or the test interval. Improving reliability: diversity (different technologies), separation (no single point of failure), fail-safe design.

    SubsystemVotingλ per channel (/yr)PFDavgShare

    The course method for parallel systems. Three layers against the same hazard, each with an equivalent failure rate (sum of its blocks), combined as parallel systems through MTTF (inclusion–exclusion): 1/λsys = Σ1/λi − Σ1/(λi+λj) + 1/(λ1+λ2+λ3).

    H-100 low feed flow: BPCS = flow sensor 1.14 + controller 0.2 + control valve 0.6; alarm = flow sensor 1.14 + controller 0.2 + operator 1.0; SIS = SIS flow sensor 0.010 + SIS controller 0.001 + shutdown valve 0.020 + solenoid 0.004. The result is set by the most reliable branch. LOPA (Part B) treats the same layers differently: it multiplies the demand rate by each layer's PFD, and it gives no credit to a layer that shares its sensor with the initiating event.

    A5 · Failure data used in this tab

    EquipmentFailure mode / contextGeneric rate (/yr)SIS / safety-grade rate (/yr)

    Sources used by the course: OREDA and the CCPS Guidelines for Initiating Events and Independent Protection Layers. A generic rate counts all failure modes; an SIS rate counts only dangerous undetected failures of certified equipment. Millions of unit-hours are needed for a confident rate.

    Part B · Layers of protection analysis (LOPA)

    B1 · The method

    1. Take a scenario from the HAZOP (cause → consequence) and rate its severity; the severity sets the target frequency.
    2. Estimate the initiating event frequency (IEF) from failure data. If several causes lead to the same consequence, work each and add the frequencies.
    3. Credit each independent protection layer (IPL) with its PFD. A layer that shares a component with the initiating event, or with another credited layer, gets no credit.
    4. Apply enabling events (time at risk) and conditional modifiers (probability of ignition, occupancy, probability of fatality).
    5. Compare with the target: RRF = f / target. If RRF > 1, the gap sets the PFD, and so the SIL, of the extra layer.

    Lecture example: pressure control malfunction 0.1 /yr × high-pressure alarm 0.1 × relief valve 0.01 × occupancy 0.1 = 10−5 /yr against a fatality target of 10−6 /yr → RRF = 10, not acceptable.

    B2 · Criteria used here (course risk matrix)

    SeverityTarget risk frequency (/yr)Health and safetyEnvironmentEconomic

    Likelihood levels by frequency: 5 most likely (~10 /yr), 4 likely (~1), 3 possible (~0.1), 2 rare (~0.01), 1 almost impossible (~0.001); the band boundaries are taken halfway between decades. Risk = severity × likelihood: 1 negligible, 2–6 low, 8–12 medium, 15–20 high, 25 extreme. Target frequencies differ by country (for a fatality about 10−4 to 10−6 /yr). This matrix is stricter than the HAZOP tab's simple S×L banding, which was used only to rank rows.

    B3 · What counts as an IPL

    An IPL must be independent of the initiating event and of the other credited layers, specific to the scenario, dependable (its PFD can be justified) and auditable (tested). Procedures, training and inspection are safeguards but usually not IPLs.

    LayerPFD credited

    B4 · H-100 LOPA worksheet

    Independent protection layers
    Conditional modifiers
    Initiating eventIEF (/yr)IPLs credited (struck = selected but not independent of this cause)ΠPFDCMFrequency (/yr)

    B5 · LOPA register

    IDScenarioSTargetf, baseRRF, basef, with recommendationsRRF, with recommendationsRecommendation

    What the numbers say: the shared transmitter FT-008 dominates everything in L1. When it fails high, FIC-003 cuts the flow, and the alarm and the trip that should catch it read the same wrong value. No SIL on the trip logic can fix a layer that is not independent. The same lesson appears in L4, where the draft trip cannot see a meter error.

    Part C · Bow-tie

    A bow-tie is several LOPAs drawn around one top event (the moment control of the hazard is lost). Threats on the left pass prevention (control) barriers; consequences on the right sit behind recovery (mitigation) barriers and conditional modifiers. Escalation factors are conditions that defeat a barrier (a bypass, a fouled sensor). The top-event frequency is the sum of the threat frequencies times their barrier PFDs. Barrier colours follow the Safety layers tab; grey is a procedure or a conditional modifier.

    Escalation factors

    3 · Blocks

    4 · Streams, design and now

    Read from the Process tab's stream table, so the two tabs always agree. Red = more than 1 % away from design.

    5 · Balances across the block boundaries

    A BFD is where balances are checked first: draw a boundary around one block or around the whole unit and compare what crosses it. At steady state in = out; during an upset the difference is the accumulation.

    6 · From BFD to PFD

    • Each block opens into its equipment: "Feed pumps" becomes P-100A and P-100B; "H-100" becomes a radiant section, a convection section, a burner and a stack.
    • Each stream gets a flag with flow, temperature and pressure from the heat and mass balance.
    • The control valves that set the process (FV-010 feed, FV-300 fuel, FV-200 air) are added, because they decide where the degrees of freedom are.
    • Utilities are drawn to the equipment that uses them (heating fluid from Unit A at E-100).
    • Next: the PFD tab, then the P&ID.

    Process flow diagram (PFD-100) · H-100

    The BFD opened up into equipment: each item has its tag and symbol, each numbered stream carries a flag with its design flow, temperature and pressure, and the control valves that set the process are shown.

    1 What a PFD adds · 2 The drawing · 3 Equipment list · 4 Flags and the model · 5 Reading the PFD · 6 What the P&ID adds

    1 · What a PFD adds to the BFD

    • Equipment symbols and tags (ISO 10628): tank, pumps, shell-and-tube exchanger, fired heater, intake screen.
    • Stream flags (Turton style): mass flow in kg/h, temperature in °C and pressure in kPa gauge, from the heat and mass balance.
    • Control valves that define the process: feed (FV-010), fuel (FV-300) and air (FV-200). They mark where the degrees of freedom are.
    • Utilities drawn to the equipment that uses them, and a title block with the drawing number, revision and notes.

    2 · The drawing

    PDFPowerPoint (editable)SVGPNGFiles in the same folder (e.g. GitHub Pages).

    3 · Equipment list

    4 · The flags beside the running model

    Drawing = the value printed on PFD-100. Design = the simulator's lined-out state. Now = live. The drawing rounds the balance, so small differences to Design are expected; Now moves with any upset. PFD-100 numbers its own streams (Turton style), so its numbers differ from the Process and BFD tabs; the matching BFD number is in brackets.

    5 · Reading the PFD

    • Two fluids never mix in E-100 (feed in the tubes, heating fluid from Unit A in the shell) or in H-100 (feed in the coil, flue gas outside it). Heat crosses the wall; mass does not.
    • Flow in = flow out on every block: the feed keeps 19 584 kg/h from stream 2 to stream 5; fuel 243 + air 3892 + in-leakage ≈ flue gas 4380 kg/h (stream 9).
    • Pressure falls along each path: the pump lifts the feed to about 1030 kPa; E-100, FV-010 and the coil use it up to about 545 kPa at the outlet to V-200. On the air side the pressure is below atmospheric all the way to the stack (natural draft).
    • No recycle: H-100 is once-through. The only heat integration is E-100 with Unit A, which is why H-100 must be able to start and run without it (Transition and Flexibility tabs).

    6 · What the P&ID adds

    • Every hand valve, block valve, drain and vent; the spare pump's piping; line numbers and sizes.
    • Every instrument and loop (FIC-003, TIC-030, FIC-005 and the indicators), with fail positions.
    • The safety system: burner management trips, shut-off valves XV-301/302 with the bleed XV-303, relief and explosion doors.
    • Next: the Control loop design and Safety layers tabs build on it, then the P&ID itself.

    Operating windows · where H-100 can run, what limits it, and how much room there is

    Teaching slide deck · Operating windows (33 slides, interactive) — operability, variability, bounds and the integrity operating window, capacity and turndown, and the Type I, II and III window worked on the H-100 model.
    Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

    Follows the course lecture Operating Windows (2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement, after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). Every window on this tab was computed on copies of this simulator's own model: 400 Type I runs and 900 Type II/III runs, each to steady state, with the trips switched off so the limits can be seen rather than cut short. The live plant is never touched. Limits come from the page's alarms (ALM), trips and controller ranges; limits marked "assumed" are for teaching.

    1 Operability · 2 Variability · 3 Bounds and IOW · 4 Worst case and point check · 5 Capacity and turndown · 6 Type I window · 7 Type II and III window · 8 Monte Carlo window · 9 Manipulated variables · 10 Holes and limitations

    1 · Operability and the operating window

    Process operability means the plant has the capacity and flexibility to reach a range of operating conditions safely, reliably, profitably, and with good dynamic performance and product quality. The operating window is the range of achievable steady-state operation: the set of process conditions for which every controlled variable can be held at its set point and no limit is broken. It is shaped by four things.

    The variables of H-100

    ClassVariable (tag)DesignWhy it is in this class

    2 · Variability: the design basis the window must cover

    "The abnormal is normal." A window is only as good as the list of changes it was sized for. The lecture's five sources of variability, written as a design basis memorandum for H-100 (ranges and frequencies are teaching values unless a tag's alarm sets them):

    SourceWhat changes on H-100Range used hereHow oftenCovered by

    A single human error must not cause an unsafe condition or environmental damage and must not stay undetected; that is why the bounds in part 3 have alarms and, where the damage is fast, trips.

    3 · Bounds and the integrity operating window

    The bounds are the frame of the window: upper and lower limits set by materials, design parameters and performance. A hard bound cannot be crossed (flame, draft, positive firebox pressure, burner pressure); a soft bound can be crossed for a while but the equipment degrades (tube-skin creep, refractory, stack). The integrity operating window (IOW) puts levels on each: target range, standard limit (failure with sustained operation) and critical limit (failure quickly). The table shows the design value, the live value and the margin to each limit.

    BoundKindWhy it existsLimitDesignNowMargin now ÷ margin at design

    Reading the IOW. Inside the target range the heater is stable and reliable. Between the target range and the standard limit it is still safe, but time counts: creep, coking and refractory damage accumulate. Past the critical limit failure is quick; that is where the trips of the Safety layers tab act. On a fired heater the hard bounds are about combustion (minimum excess air, draft, flame) and the soft bounds about metal temperature (tube skin, supports, stack).

    4 · Design for the worst case, and a live point check

    Equipment is sized for the worst case of the variability it must handle. For a heat exchanger (Q = UA F ΔTlm) the worst case is the highest flow at the highest temperature with the most fouling. For H-100 each piece of equipment has its own worst case. Pick one, or set your own point, and the page runs this model to steady state (TIC-030 at 350 °C, O₂ held at 2.0 %, trips off) and checks every bound.

    5 · Capacity and turndown

    A small plant that only just meets the design point is cheap but has no window; a large one has a window but costs capital and runs inefficiently at low rate. The lecture's rule: the capacity must be safe, protect expensive equipment and meet quality for the base case and frequently occurring variability; lower production is acceptable in rare cases; stop for extreme ones. Turndown ratio = normal maximum ÷ normal minimum, where "normal" means sustainable without hazard or damage.

    Each piece of equipment has its own feed range. The heater's range is the overlap of all of them, so it is always smaller than any single element's. Ranges below are at the design TI-010 (180 °C), 20 °C ambient and the design damper, from the Type III grid of part 7; instrument ranges use the usual 25–100 % of span for an orifice meter.

    ElementTurndown or rangeability on H-100Typical (lecture)Flexibility class

    6 · Steady-state operating window, Type I: what the handles can reach

    The lecture writes the model as y = A u + B d + C (y controlled variables, u manipulated, d disturbances) and poses three problems:

    TypeGivenFindOn H-100
    Iu over its range; d and parameters fixedachievable y (set points reachable without disturbances)FV-300 fuel valve × FV-200 air valve, 5–100 %, feed 6.8 L/s, TI-010 180 °C → outlet temperature and O₂
    IIy at set point; d over its rangeu needed for each doutlet 350 °C, O₂ 2.0 %; feed 3–10 L/s × TI-010 130–220 °C → FV-300 and FV-200 openings
    IIIy at set point; u within its ranged that can be correctedthe feed and TI-010 combinations the heater can absorb, and which bound stops it

    Type I is calculated in causal order (valves → firing → temperatures), like the lecture's blending example. Each cell below is one steady state with both valves in manual.

    outlined cells = every bound met · ✕ = flame out

    What Type I shows. The reachable set of (outlet temperature, O₂) is not a rectangle: the air valve moves O₂ and the fuel valve moves temperature, but each moves both. Along a row of constant fuel, the outlet temperature peaks near λ ≈ 1 and falls on either side: too little air caps the heat release by oxygen, too much air carries heat up the stack. Left of the peak (fuel-rich) more fuel lowers the temperature, so the same outlet temperature can be reached at two air openings. Only the lean side is inside the window.

    7 · Type II and Type III: the disturbances H-100 can absorb

    Now the controlled variables sit at their set points (TIC-030 350 °C, O₂ 2.0 % by adjusting the air) while the disturbances move. Type II reads the handle positions each disturbance needs; Type III keeps only the points where every handle is inside its range and every bound holds, and colours the rest by the bound that fails first.

    8 · Monte Carlo operating window

    The lecture's recipe: (1) simulate the base case, (2) replace the uncertain inputs by samples from their distributions and repeat, (3) mark each sample feasible or infeasible against every bound, (4) report the fraction and show it graphically. Here the samples are interpolated in the grid of part 7 (feed, TI-010 and ambient) at the damper chosen above.

    9 · Manipulated variables: enough, strong, independent, fast

    With n adjustable handles and m variables to hold: n = m gives a finite window with each point exactly specified; n < m gives no window (at best the design point) and is not an acceptable design; n > m leaves extra freedom (several ways to reach a point, which can be used to optimise).

    Held variable (m)Handle (n)Steady-state gain of the handle (+5 % output, all loops in manual)
    Lecture criterionCheck on H-100

    10 · Holes in the window, and what the steady-state window does not tell you

    • Only steady states. Transients leave the window for a while: a feed step from 6.8 to 8.0 L/s dips the outlet about 12 °C for several minutes (Flexibility tab, part 7) although 8.0 L/s is inside the window.
    • Large excursions are outside the method: light-off, purge, trips and shutdown have their own procedures and limits (BMS tab).
    • One steady state per case is assumed. Part 6 shows H-100 has two air openings for the same outlet temperature at a fixed fuel valve; the analysis keeps the lean one.
    • Model structure is assumed right. Fouling, coking, burner wear and meter errors change A, B and C; the window shrinks. Re-run it with the faults you expect.
    • Curse of dimensionality. Three disturbances at 15 × 10 × 3 points and two damper positions took 900 runs; every added variable multiplies that.

    References: T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials (2013); course lecture 2105625 Operating Windows; API RP 584 Integrity Operating Windows; API 560 Fired Heaters for General Refinery Service; API RP 556 Instrumentation, Control and Protective Systems for Gas Fired Heaters.

    Flexibility · the handles that steer H-100 through its operating window

    Teaching slide deck · Flexibility (30 slides, interactive) — how many handles, where to put them, flexibility for fluid flow, heat transfer and production rate, and the fired heater's air–fuel flexibility, worked on the H-100 model.
    Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

    Follows the course lecture Flexibility (2105625 Process Analysis and Improvement, after T. Marlin's Process Operability class materials). The Operating windows tab finds where H-100 can run; this tab looks at the handles that move it there. Gains, capacities and responses come from runs on copies of this simulator's model; the pump and valve curves in part 4a are an illustration calibrated to the design point and are marked so.

    1 What flexibility is · 2 How many · 3 Where · 4 Fluid flow · 5 Heat transfer · 6 Production rate · 7 Air and fuel · 8 How much · 9 Recommendations

    1 · What flexibility is

    Flexibility is the ability of a plant to operate reliably across a wide range of rates and conditions without losing quantity or quality. Some controlled variables are held at their set points while disturbances arrive; flexibility is what lets us steer the process after the equipment has been built.

    Without flexibility the process does not respond to set-point changes and passes every disturbance on to quality, rate and safety. With flexibility it reaches its set points and compensates the disturbances.

    How it is provided

    • Spare capacity in pumps, valves, exchangers, vessels, motor speed.
    • Adjustable utility flows: cooling water, steam, fuel, air, N₂, H₂.
    • By-passes that send part of a flow around equipment.

    Four design questions: how many handles, where, which tools (valves, speed), and how much capacity.

    The flexibility register of H-100

    HandleWhat it adjustsKind of flexibilityAt designSpare at designStatus

    2 · How many handles? Degrees of freedom

    A successful design needs number of adjustable valves ≥ number of variables to be held. The maximum number of controlled variables equals the degrees of freedom, and the minimum number of handles equals the number of variables we insist on.

    Variable H-100 must holdWhyHandle used

    3 · Where? Causal paths from each handle

    Each held variable needs a handle with an independent causal path to it. Interaction is allowed as long as every desired point can still be reached. The lecture's three cases:

    Steady-state effect of +5 % on each handle, all loops in manual, run on the model (the numbers behind the causal map):

    Interaction without dependence: fuel and air

    Fuel and air both move the outlet temperature and the O₂, but not in the same ratio, so any nearby (temperature, O₂) pair can be reached. Ask for a change and the page solves the 2 × 2 steady-state model for the valve moves:

    A linked pair on H-100. E-100 has one handle, HV-063. With the feed rate fixed by production, the heat duty is fixed once TI-010 is chosen, and so is the heating-fluid return temperature to Unit A: Q = Ffeedcp(T010 − T0) = Fhotcp,h(Th,in − Th,out). The two temperatures are "connected by a beam"; holding both needs a second handle (part 5).

    4 · Flexibility for fluid flow

    For liquids the flow settles where the pump's pressure rise equals the losses: F = √(ΔP / ((fL/D + Kvalve + ΣKj) ρ/2g)). Only the valve term (or the pump speed) is adjustable. Three flows on H-100 show three kinds of flexibility.

    4a · Feed: valve throttling or pump speed (illustration)

    Pump curve from the page's PI-002 relation (1400 − 8F² kPa at full speed, affinity laws for speed); coil loss from PI-009; 350 kPa delivery pressure and an equal-percentage FV-010 (R = 30) are assumed so that design falls at 57 % open. The simulator itself treats FV-010 as linear.

    4b · Fuel oil: FV-300 in series with the burner gun (the model's own equation)

    W = √(Ps / (1/Kv² + 1/Kn²)) with Kv = 14.3·x (FV-300) and Kn = 9.93 (gun). The gun takes most of the pressure, so the installed characteristic is strongly curved: the last 30 % of valve travel adds little fuel. Supply pressure and gun condition set the capacity, not the valve.

    4c · Combustion air: natural draft, no fan

    5 · Flexibility for heat transfer

    Q = U A ΔT*: flexibility can act on U (a flow changes the film coefficient), on A (level in a kettle, active area), or on ΔT (a utility's temperature or flow, a by-pass that mixes).

    Heat-transfer duty on H-100UAΔT*Handle today
    Radiant section (≈ 69 % of duty)radiation, set by flame and wall temperaturefixed coil(Tfirebox4 − Ttube4): moved by firingFV-300 fuel: a utility flow
    Convection section (≈ 31 %)flue gas flowfixed bank; fouling lowers Uflue gas temperaturenone (follows firing and air)
    E-100 preheaterheating-fluid flowfixedheating-fluid temperature and flowHV-063: the hot-side flow

    The lecture's three cases, applied to E-100 (goal: hold TI-010)

    CaseFeed (cold)Heating fluid (hot)FlexibilityOn H-100
    afixed by productionadjustableadjust the hot flowAs built: HV-063. The return temperature to Unit A then floats.
    badjustablefixedadjusting the feed flow is not done (its flow matters too); by-pass part of the feed around E-100 and mixRecommended: feed by-pass with a three-way valve (0–100 %), TIC on TI-010. Fast (mixing).
    cfixedfixed (Unit A needs its flow)by-pass on the hot sideRecommended if Unit A must keep its circulation: hot-side three-way valve.

    Model relation: ε = 0.737·min(√(x/60), 1.3), TI-010 = T₀ + ε(Th − T₀) with T₀ = 40 °C and Th = 230 °C; the by-passed feed rejoins at 40 °C. The simulator does not raise ε when less feed passes E-100, so the by-pass curve is slightly pessimistic.

    6 · Flexibility for production rate

    At steady state material must balance in every unit and the whole plant (no long-term accumulation). One flexible variable sets the rate; every other flow follows automatically without people, and measured flows are never simply matched to each other (meter errors would accumulate). Level and pressure show inventory; on H-100 the liquid-full coil has no inventory to control.

    Guiding principleH-100

    Move the feed and TI-010: the bars show how open each handle must be to hold 350 °C and 2 % O₂ (Type II runs of the Operating windows tab, 20 °C, damper 67 %). The first bar to reach 95 % is the capacity that sets the top of the window.

      Teaching slide deck · C&E matrix (24 slides, interactive) — how a cause and effect matrix is built and read, the H-100 trip sequence second by second, first-out replayed on runs of the model, spotting errors and checking sensor independence.

      Every alarm and trip of the heater in one sheet: the causes down the left (tag, service, direction, setting, unit, note), the final elements and annunciation across the top, and an X where a cause drives an effect. It is the document the instrument engineer programs the logic solver from and the operator reads to know what a trip will do. The live column shows which causes are active in the running simulator.

      Cause and effect diagram, PDF (A3)Document NDFH-V1-IN-CE-001 rev R0. The same data builds this table and the PDF.
      1 What a C&E diagram is · 2 The diagram · 3 How to read a row · 4 Notes · 5 Checks against the simulator

      1 · What a cause and effect diagram is

      • A cause is one sensed condition with its direction and setting (low, low-low, high, high-high, flame lost, push-button). Alarm-only causes light the amber lamp and sound the horn; trip causes act on the final elements and light the red lamp.
      • An effect is one action on one device, written as a code in the header row (C close, O open, FO fully open, OFF, TP tripped). The X marks which causes drive it.
      • The matrix is written from the SRS of each SIF (next to this tab) and from the alarm list; it must match the logic exactly. On H-100 the effects come from the simulator's trip function, so they cannot drift.

      2 · The diagram

      3 · How to read a row

      • FSLL-008, Low-Low 3.4 L/s, 5 s: after 5 s below 3.4 L/s the logic closes XV-301 and XV-302, opens the bleed XV-303, puts TIC-030 in MAN at 0 % (FV-300 closes), drives FIC-005 and HIC-400 to 100 % to sweep the firebox, cancels any trial for ignition, latches the BMS in TRIPPED with FSLL-008 as first-out, and lights the red lamp with the horn.
      • PIAL-030, Low 1.5 mmH₂O: alarm only (amber lamp and horn); the trip on the same transmitter is the separate row PSLL-030 at 0.5 mmH₂O, armed only when firing.
      • A trip is cleared only from the BMS when its cause is gone, and the burner is lit again only after a full purge.
