        1 · What a transition is, and which ones H-100 has

        Transitions are planned transient behaviour between different initial and final conditions. They need their own procedures, strategies, process structure and sometimes extra equipment, because the plant was designed for the steady state.

        KindWhen it happensOn H-100Part

        2 · Before startup: the plant is made ready

        Done before the procedure starts (lecture list, applied to H-100):

          Extra equipment and features that exist only for transitions:

          ItemWhy a transition needs it

          A real heater startup takes hours to days (refractory dry-out alone can take a day on a new lining). The simulator compresses a warm restart into one to four hours of simulated time.

          3 · Startup from cold: the order and the reasons

          No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

          How fast should the outlet be brought up? The same script was run with the TIC-030 set point stepped to 350 °C, and ramped at 1, 2 and 5 °C/min:

          4 · Shutdown: remove the heat first, keep the heat sink last

          No.StepWhy this order (analysis)Safety concern

          5 · Regeneration and maintenance transitions

          Catalysts lose activity, adsorbents fill, and surfaces foul or coke: they need periodic regeneration, often under different feeds and conditions that can be hazardous (introducing oxygen where there is normally hydrocarbon, exothermic burns). The lecture's three strategies: parallel equipment (one regenerates while the other runs), storage (the rest of the plant runs from a tank while the unit is out), or shutdown.

          Regeneration or maintenance on H-100WhyWhat changesHazards and how they are handledStrategy

          How big must the storage be?

          With a single heater, the units before and after H-100 keep running only if tanks hold the flow for the whole outage: holdup time V/F ≥ shutdown time. The inventory is adjusted just before the shutdown (upstream tank drawn down, downstream tank filled).

          6 · Blocked operation: campaigns and fast changeovers

          When the same equipment makes several products, it runs in blocks of steady operation separated by transitions. Material made during the transition is worth less or nothing, so transitions should be expedited, and product must be stored to meet demand. For H-100, suppose the downstream unit alternates between a campaign at 350 °C and one at 330 °C. Off-specification time is counted while the outlet is more than 2 °C away from the new target:

          7 · Load following: H-100 feeds a unit that sets its own rate

          A supplier that feeds consumers without storage must follow the load in time. The lecture's steam example: do not sum the measured demands (errors accumulate); control the header pressure and let generation follow it. For H-100 the downstream unit asks for more feed; the question is how fast the heater can follow without upsetting the outlet or the combustion. Feed moved 6.8 → 8.2 L/s with the air on ratio control:

          Lecture's industrial practice (steam)Same idea on H-100

          8 · Batch processes, and what makes transitions hard

          Batch operation (all material at the start) and semi-batch (some added later) never reach a steady state: every batch is a transition, used for small quantities, high purity or long residence times (food, pharmaceuticals, fine chemicals, fermentation), with storage between batch and continuous sections. H-100 is continuous, so its transitions are the ones above.

          • The control system must follow the desired path, not just hold a point: set-point ramps, low-fire stops, ratio control that keeps air ahead of fuel.
          • Non-linear over a wide range: at low rate the coil holds the liquid longer (τ ≈ 90 s × 6.8/F) and the same fuel move changes the outlet more, so a tuning chosen at design behaves differently at startup rates.
          • Protection during transitions: permissives replace trips while the plant is not yet running (purge permissives, flame proving), and several trips are only armed once firing (PSLL-020, PSLL-030, BSLL-005).

          References: course lecture Operating during Transition and Process Startup Workshop (Process Operation); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; API 560 and API RP 556 (fired heaters, their controls and protective systems); NFPA 86 (purge and light-off); API RP 573 (inspection of fired heaters, decoking).

          Process reliability · how long H-100 runs between outages, and how to make it run longer

          Teaching slide deck · Process reliability (28 slides, interactive) — reliability, failure rate and availability, series, parallel, standby and k-out-of-N structures on H-100, design and operation for reliability, inventory, maintenance and life-cycle cost.
          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          Follows the course material on reliability: T. Marlin's Operability in Process Design, Chapter 4 Reliability (lecture and chapter), the Introduction to Reliability Engineering course (failure statistics, MTTF/MTBF, series/parallel/k-of-n models, critical items) and the fired-heater reliability notes (the heater audit items and the burner-plugging incident). The LOPA tab treats reliability of safeguards (probability of failure on demand); this tab treats reliability of production: outages cost money, not lives. Failure rates are the course's generic all-modes values; fractions, repair times and costs marked "assumed" are teaching values.

          1 Definitions · 2 Failure rate and life · 3 Structures · 4 H-100 as a series system · 5 Design for reliability · 6 Operating for reliability · 7 Inventory · 8 Maintenance · 9 Life-cycle cost · 10 Fired-heater reliability audit

          1 · Reliability, availability and why they differ

          TermDefinitionOn H-100

          Availability is not reliability. A heater that trips twelve times a year but relights in ten minutes each time has 99.98 % availability and poor reliability; every trip is a purge, a light-off and a thermal cycle on the tubes. The course example: three years of the same plant with uptimes 6815, 7612 and 8471 h of 8760 h.

          2 · Failure rate, the bathtub and the exponential model

          Failure rate λ(t) = failures per unit time divided by the items still working. Over life it often follows the bathtub: infant mortality (falling λ), chance failures (constant λ), wear-out (rising λ). Most real equipment does not follow the full bathtub (the RCM studies show six patterns, most with no wear-out), so the right maintenance depends on the pattern. With constant λ:

          R(t) = e−λt,   F(t) = 1 − R(t),   MTTF = 1/λ

          At t = MTTF only 37 % survive (63.2 % have failed). The course example: λ = 0.0001 /h → MTTF 10 000 h; R(5000 h) = e−0.5 = 0.61; expected outages in 5000 h = 0.5.

          3 · Structures: series, parallel, standby, k out of N

          A plant is many components joined in structures; the structure sets the system reliability. All formulas assume independent failures (no common cause) and, for standby, perfect switching.

          StructureWorks whenReliabilityMTTF (identical elements, λ each)H-100 example

          Course workshop check: four identical elements at λ = 4×10⁻³ /h give MTTF 62.5 h in series, 521 h in parallel and 1000 h as one running plus three standby.

          A standby is only as good as its switch-over time. The chapter's warning fits H-100 exactly: combustion cannot ride through a loss of flow, so when P-100A trips, FSLL-008 trips the burner after 5 s, long before an operator can start P-100B. The spare shortens the outage (repair time) but does not prevent it, unless P-100B starts automatically within seconds (hot standby).

          4 · H-100 as a series system: what stops the heater, and how often

          For production every element in the chain feed pump → feed valve → coil → fuel train → burner → air and draft → trips must work, so H-100 is a series system: λsys = Σ λi × fi, where fi is the fraction of element i's failures that stop the heater (a spurious trip, a lost flame, a lost pump). Toggle design changes and see the effect on outages, availability and cost.

          5 · Design for reliability

          Lecture principleWhat it meansH-100 as builtGap or recommendation

          "There is no safe side in equipment sizing." An oversized pump runs far left of its best-efficiency point: recirculation, vibration, seal and bearing failures ("pumps don't die; engineers kill them"). The same holds for an oversized burner gun: low atomising pressure, poor flame, coke on the tip.

          6 · Operating for reliability: short-term gain against long-term life

          The lecture's turbo-generator: a hotter superheat raises efficiency but, above the alarm, the turbine failure rate climbs. On H-100 the same trade-off sits on the tube skin: firing harder (more feed, colder feed, coke) raises TI-024 and consumes creep life. Moving a variable toward a constraint must be combined with reducing its variability.

          Creep rule of thumb (assumed for teaching): tube life halves for every 15 °C of metal temperature; life is referred to the design skin temperature of 398 °C; 480 °C is the assumed critical limit from the Safety layers tab.

          7 · Reliability through inventory

          A tank between an unreliable unit and the next one lets the next unit keep running while the first is repaired. With the upstream unit's repair time exponentially distributed (mean MTTR) and a holdup time τ = V/F, the chance that one outage is covered by the tank is 1 − e−τ/MTTR. The lecture's example: P1 reliability 0.15, P2 reliability 0.95.

          Inventory has a price: working capital, tank cost, hazardous inventory, product degradation. The chapter's Tables 4.1 and 4.2 list the reasons for and against; the engineer places inventory next to the unreliable units and sizes it for their repair times.

          8 · Maintenance for reliability

          Strategy (NASA RCM)IdeaH-100 items that suit it

          9 · Life-cycle cost: how many feed pumps?

          Life-cycle costing adds to the usual profitability analysis the costs that reliability changes: maintenance and spares, failure frequency, the cost of each failure (repair, lost production, restart) and the extra equipment for redundancy. The lecture's example asks how many pumps in standby (1 to 4). Costs below are assumed teaching values; the restart time comes from the Transition operation tab (purge, light-off and warm-up about 1 h at the fastest safe ramp).

          10 · Fired-heater reliability audit applied to H-100

          A refinery furnace team audits eight reliability drivers before failures occur. The same checks on H-100, with the model's numbers where it has them:

          DriverWhy it mattersH-100

          Case to remember. In a published 2003 incident at a petrochemical plant, newly fitted low-NOx burners plugged with coke and iron oxide; the flames became unstable, and while operators adjusted the air damper and registers to steady them, fuel accumulated in an oxygen-poor firebox and exploded, destroying the heater. Lessons: hazard-review new burner technology, prove it by performance tests, clean fuel lines before commissioning, and treat an unstable flame as a reason to trip, not to tune.

          References: T. Marlin, Operability in Process Design, Ch. 4 Reliability (2013); H.P. Barringer, Life Cycle Cost Tutorial (1996); CCPS, Guidelines for Process Equipment Reliability Data (1989); NASA, Reliability Centered Maintenance Guide (2000); B.S. Dhillon, Reliability, Quality and Safety for Engineers (2005); API 560, API RP 573 and API RP 530 (tube design and creep).

          Efficiency · where H-100's fuel goes, and how to burn less of it

          Teaching slide deck · Efficiency (25 slides, interactive) — what efficiency means and where it sits among the priorities, the heater's efficiency by the direct and the indirect method, excess air and stack temperature, heat recovery, pump energy, constraint pushing and an energy dashboard, all on the H-100 model.
          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          Follows the course lecture Process Efficiency (Process Operation) and the industry talk Efficiency Energy Practices in Petrochemical Plant (2025). Curves marked "model" are steady states of this simulator (TIC-030 at 350 °C, O₂ or air held, trips off); rules of thumb are quoted from the talk and compared with the model; prices and investment costs are assumed teaching values you can change.

          1 Efficiency and priorities · 2 H-100 efficiency now · 3 Excess air · 4 Stack temperature · 5 Heat recovery · 6 Fuel-saving options · 7 Pump energy · 8 Operating conditions · 9 Energy monitoring

          1 · Efficiency, optimisation and their place among the priorities

          Efficiency (in operation, the same as optimisation) is good economic performance: better quality or rate, less raw material, effluent and energy, and lower environmental impact (greenhouse gas, pollution). For energy: efficiency = useful energy output ÷ total energy input, and a chain of steps multiplies: boiler 90 % × turbo-generator 40 % × transmission 90 % = 32.4 %.

          Four ways to get it (lecture): design with the right capacities; use existing equipment in the most efficient way; choose better process structures (recycle, recover energy); choose the best operating conditions inside the window.

          PriorityObjectiveOn H-100

          2 · H-100 efficiency now: direct and indirect method

          Direct method: η = heat absorbed by the process ÷ heat in the fuel. Indirect method: η = 100 % − losses (stack gas, incomplete combustion, casing). The indirect method is preferred when the absorbed duty is hard to measure. Both are computed live from the running simulator.

          3 · Excess air: the first 1–3 % of fuel

          Combustion needs some excess air to burn completely, but every extra kilogram of air is heated to stack temperature and thrown away. Excess air from the flue analysis: %E = %O₂ × 100 / (21 − %O₂) (dry). Tramp air leaking in through peep doors and the casing raises the O₂ without helping combustion.

          4 · Stack temperature: the other big loss

          The talk's rule: every 35 °F (19 °C) lower flue gas temperature saves about 1 % fuel. On H-100 the model's convection-fouling fault raises the stack by lowering the convection pickup; the fuel follows.

          5 · Process structure: heat recovery

          The lecture's third approach: recover energy (feed–effluent exchange, preheat), recycle material. H-100 already recovers heat twice: E-100 preheats the feed with Unit A's hot fluid, and the convection section recovers flue-gas heat. What each is worth, from the model:

          The lecture's warning applies: full heat integration leaves no flexibility and no way to start up; E-100 needs its own handle (HV-063) and H-100 must be able to fire without it (Flexibility and Transition tabs).

          6 · Fuel-saving options for a fired heater, sized for H-100

          Typical improvements quoted in the talk, and an estimate for H-100 at the fuel price you set. The air preheater is estimated from an energy balance (not in the simulator); the rest scale the model's design fuel.

          7 · Design with the right capacity: pump energy

          An oversized constant-speed pump reaches its flow only by burning pressure in a control valve. A variable-speed drive (VSD) removes the throttling; the affinity laws give flow ∝ speed, head ∝ speed², power ∝ speed³. Shaft power = ρ g Q H / ηpump; motor efficiency 0.80–0.95. The P-100 curve is the Flexibility tab's illustration calibrated to design.

          8 · Best operating conditions: push toward the constraint

          Many conditions do not affect safety or quality but do affect profit; the best value is usually against a constraint, and how close you can go depends on variability (the lecture's cracking furnace: maximise conversion but never exceed 864 °C). For H-100 the constraint is minimum O₂: below about 1 % the CO climbs. A tighter controller (less σ) lets the set point move down.

          Industrial practice: optimise slowly (a fast optimiser disturbs quality), from a model when one exists and from careful plant tests when not; the stack-O₂ systems quoted in the talk report about 5 % fuel saving mainly from steadier operation.

          9 · Energy monitoring: key energy variables for H-100

          A plant energy dashboard tracks the specific energy consumption (SEC, energy per unit of product) against its benchmark and the key energy variables (KEV) that move it. Live from the simulator:

          Key energy variableTargetNowEffect on fuel

          References: course lecture Process Efficiency (Process Operation); Efficiency Energy Practices in Petrochemical Plant (2025); T. Marlin, Process Operability class materials; API 560 (heater efficiency, calculated on LHV); US DOE Improving Process Heating System Performance.

          1 What an SOP is · 2 Format · 3 SOP register · 4 SOP viewer · 5 Writing rules · 6 Life of an SOP

          1 · What an SOP is, and which activities need one

          A standard operating procedure is the written, approved way to carry out one task: the same steps, in the same order, with the same checks, whoever is on shift. It turns the reasons worked out on the other tabs (startup order, operating window, bounds, trips) into actions an operator can follow under pressure.

          Required by process safety management (OSHA 29 CFR 1910.119(f): initial startup, normal operation, temporary operation, emergency shutdown, emergency operation, normal shutdown, startup after an emergency shutdown or turnaround; operating limits, consequences of deviation and steps to correct or avoid them; safety systems and their functions). Reviewed and certified as current at a fixed interval, and trained on.

          Design pressure is set above the highest pressure the equipment can see in operation, including upsets that are not relieved. For the coil and E-100 tube side that is the pump shut-off: P-100 can push 1400 kPa(g) against a closed valve, plus the suction pressure. Design metal temperature of a fired tube follows API 530: the highest calculated or measured tube-metal temperature plus a 15 °C allowance.

          Vapour or gas: A = W/(C Kd P1 Kb Kc) √(T Z/M), C = 0.03948 √(k (2/(k+1))(k+1)/(k−1)), Kd 0.975

          5 · Model relief runs

          Each run starts from design on a copy of the H-100 model, applies one failure with no operator action, and runs for 10 min, once with the trips disabled (what the relief device would have to handle) and once with the SIS active. The model does not compute vessel pressures above the pump curve, so pressures are read from the pump and fuel-supply relations; temperatures and trips come from the full model. Watch the minimum outlet as well as the maximum: a fuel valve failing open with the air unchanged makes the firing fuel-rich, so the outlet falls while CO climbs (the HAZOP tab found the same).

          6 · Inlet loss and back pressure

          A relief valve chatters if the pressure loss in its inlet line is more than 3 % of set, and a conventional valve loses capacity if the built-up back pressure exceeds 10 % of set (50 % for a balanced bellows valve, API 520 Part II). Try the inlet and outlet of PSV-101.

          Open the electrical load list (PDF)

          A natural-draft heater needs little power: no fans, so the feed pumps are almost the whole load. The electrical lessons on this unit are about which loads must not stop (the SIS de-energises to trip, so its power supply must be reliable or a power dip becomes a trip) and where electrical equipment may be placed near flammable liquids. Absorbed pump power comes from the model's pump curve.

          1 Load list · 2 Maximum demand · 3 Cable sizing · 4 Power for the SIS and DCS · 5 Hazardous areas · 6 Checks

          1 · Load list

          2 · Maximum demand

          Maximum demand = Σ continuous + 0.3 Σ intermittent + 0.1 Σ standby (typical diversity factors). The spare pump counts only as standby because the two pumps never run together for long.

          3 · Cable sizing

          Copper, PVC/XLPE multicore, resistance at 70 °C and current ratings typical of IEC 60364-5-52 tables (A10); use the project's cable tables and derating for a real design. Criteria: running voltage drop ≤ 5 %, starting voltage drop ≤ 15 %.

          4 · Power for the SIS and DCS

          The SIS is de-energise-to-trip: XV-301 and XV-302 close when their solenoids lose power. A dip on an unprotected supply would trip the heater, so the logic solver, solenoids and flame scanner run from a UPS; the DCS and its transmitters likewise. The battery must hold the loads long enough for an orderly shutdown.

          5 · Hazardous-area schedule

          Areas are classified by how often a flammable atmosphere can be present (IEC 60079-10-1, API RP 505). Fluid properties are assumed (A7, A8). The heater itself is a source of ignition, so the classification does not protect against a leak of hot feed above its auto-ignition temperature: fire protection, emergency isolation and layout do.

          6 · Checks against the model and the other documents

          Open the commissioning plan (PDF)

          After the documents are issued, equipment is bought, inspected, installed and tested, and the plant is handed over system by system. Many start-up incidents on fired heaters come from skipped steps in this phase: a refractory heated too fast, a trip never tested, a valve installed the wrong way round. The start-up itself is the one practised on the simulator.

          Hydrotest pressures follow the codes named in the table (test factor × design pressure; the stress-ratio correction for hot design is left out here). The C&E function test proves every row of the cause and effect sheet end to end, from the field sensor to the final element.

          4 · Refractory dry-out

          New castable refractory holds water. Heated too fast, the steam spalls it. The vendor sets the curve; a typical one is shown. The model gives a reason why a dry-out often needs a temporary burner: at minimum fire with feed flowing, the H-100 burner already lifts the outlet to about 280 °C (Transition operation tab), so the slow early ramps and holds below that are hard to follow with the main burner alone.

          5 · Commissioning and start-up

          The commissioning steps after pre-commissioning, each tied to the procedure on the simulator that practises it and to the SOP that would be written for the plant.

          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          The P&ID says what is connected to what; the layout says where it stands. A plot plan places every item at true scale by spacing rules (fire, access, maintenance, escape), the elevations set the levels, and the isometrics route each line in three dimensions with its valves and supports. H-100 has no real plot plan, so this one was generated from the equipment list NDFH-V1-ME-EQL-001 and the Design tab, with spacing taken from typical practice (assumed, not a code). The same file, layout.json, builds the 3-D plant on the Visual plant 3D tab.

          1 · Plot plan

          Click an item on the plan.

          2 · Elevations and levels

          South elevation (looking north). H-100 stands on 2.0 m legs so that the burner can be reached from below (API 560 practice for floor-fired heaters); the peep doors are reached from a platform at 4.0 m and the convection headers, the damper and the stack instruments from a platform at the bottom of the convection section. Every instrument and hand valve is listed with the floor it is read or worked from.

          3 · Isometrics

          An isometric draws one line at 30° in three dimensions with every change of direction, its elevations, the valves and instruments on it, and a bill of materials. The ones below are generated from the pipe routes in the layout; a piping designer would add supports, welds and spool breaks.

          4 · From layout to the 3-D model

          The 3-D plant is built from layout.json: equipment boxes and cylinders at the plot-plan positions, the pipe routes of the isometrics, the platforms and ladders, a tag box on every instrument and hand valve at its true height, and the walking route of the outside operator. Each station of the route is a place where the operator stops, reads gauges and works valves.

          1 · How to walk the plant

          The plant is drawn from the plot plan of the Layout & isometrics tab at true scale, and every reading and valve is live: what you see is the simulator running now. Follow the yellow arrows from station to station (Next ▶), or walk freely with the pad (▲ ▼ turn ⟲ ⟳, look ⤒ ⤓) or by dragging in the picture. At each station the card on the right lists what to read (◀ Read zooms to the gauge) and what to operate (◀ Operate opens the valve panel). Everything you do is written to the event log, so the exercises can see that you went out and looked. A natural-draft heater is checked mostly by eye: the flame through the peep door, the colour of the stack, the gauges that are not on the DCS.

          2 · Identification

          Set Labels to Identify: the tag boxes go blank. Type the tag of each item at the station, then check. The aim is 90 % or better over at least three stations.

          3 · Rounds sheet

          Walk the round and fill in what the plant shows now. Readings are checked against the live plant within 3 % (or the reading resolution); states must match. A real rounds sheet is how a change is noticed before the DCS alarms.

          4 · Gauge locations by level

          5 · Hand valves

          Hand valves are on the P&ID (NDFH-V1-PID-001 rev E) and in the model: closing one does what it would do in the plant. Car-sealed (CSO) and locked (LC) valves cannot be worked from the round; they need a permit.

          Systematic problem solving · the Woods troubleshooting workbook on the simulator

          Teaching slide deck · Systematic problem solving (34 slides, interactive) — the course Woods workbook on the simulator: Stage 0 facts only, Review, Engage (run, safe-park or shut down), Define with SMARTS-$ and IS / IS NOT, Explore with balances, AND / OR and time sequence, Plan with S / D / N, P × S × T and V = I / C, Do it with decision analysis, Look back with an engineered barrier, and pulling the OTS data into the workbook.
          Open the deck (claude.ai)Open the deck (same folder, e.g. GitHub Pages)

          Troubleshooting is a method, not a flash of insight. The course workbook (Woods Troubleshooting Workbook v3, the same one used in 2105412) takes a case through Woods's stages: the problem as observed, Engage, Define, Explore, Plan, Do it and Look back, with data before action, facts apart from opinions, every hypothesis with a test that could refute it, and a check that the fix met the target. It is embedded below on the H-100 unit, with its ten Think EQUIPPED cases, tags and drawing, and a From this OTS (live) card that pulls the running simulator's trends, readings against design and event log straight in as datasets.

          1 The stages · 2 How to use it with a case · 3 The workbook

          1 · The stages

          StageThe question it answersSub-steps in the workbookWhere the simulator helps

          2 · How to use it with a case

          1. Load a Think EQUIPPED case on the Exercises tab and let it run; watch the DCS as an operator would.
          2. On the workbook Home page pick the same case, fill in the team, then work Stage 0 to Stage 6 in order (worksheet mode shows the graded sub-steps; full mode shows them all).
          3. Press Pull the run data, Pull readings now vs design and Pull the event log in "From this OTS (live)" whenever you need evidence; pin the trends on the Data page.
          4. Write each test's prediction and decision criterion in Stage 4 before you run it on the OTS, then record the verdict in 5.0.
          5. Save the project file and export the report and slides from the Output page; hand them in with the Debrief grade.

          3 · The workbook

          Trainee workbook · Natural Draft Fired Heater Ver 1

          Work through Parts A to I in order; they follow the learning path on the How to use tab. Record your answers and evidence (screenshots, CSV files) as you go; your report is built from them.

          1 Purpose · 2 The unit · 3 Control scheme · 4 Safety systems · 5 Operating rules · 6 Activities A–I · 7 Grading · 8 Report checklist

          1 · Purpose

          This workbook trains you to operate, monitor and troubleshoot a natural-draft, single-burner fired heater (H-100) that heats a hydrocarbon feed ahead of a packed-bed reactor. By the end you should be able to:

          1. Read the P&ID and the DCS displays and state the normal value and alarm limits of every key tag.
          2. Explain how heat release, air, draft and outlet temperature are connected, and predict the direction every key variable moves after a disturbance.
          3. Start up the heater safely through the burner management system (BMS) and line it out at design.
          4. Recognise an abnormal situation from alarms and trends, make it safe first, then find the root cause with a systematic six-stage method.
          5. Propose a permanent control improvement and support it with exported data.

          2 · The unit

          Feed from TK-101 is pumped by P-100A (P-100B spare), preheated in E-100 by heating fluid from Unit A (HV-063), and flow-controlled by FIC-003 through FV-010. It enters the convection coil at the top of H-100, crosses over to the radiant coil, and leaves at the bottom to the packed-bed reactor V-200. One oil burner fires upward from the floor. Combustion air is drawn in by the stack (natural draft) through the F-100 intake screen, FV-200 and the windbox. Stack damper HV-400 sets how strong the draft is.

          Values are the model's design point with noise off. Typical lined-out readings on the console differ by a few tenths.

          3 · Control scheme (P&ID rev A)

          LoopMeasuresMovesValve on air failureNotes
          FIC-003Feed flow (same meter as FIAL-008 / FSLL-008)FV-010Fail openKeeps the coil cooled if the signal is lost.
          TIC-030Outlet temperature TT-040FV-300 fuel valveFail closedIts only output is fuel. It cannot see the air.
          FIC-005Combustion air flowFV-200 air valveFail openIn rev A its set point is typed by the operator and does not follow fuel.
          HV-400—Stack damperFail openHand-set, normally 67 % open. Sets the draft that pulls air in.
          HV-063—E-100 heating fluid—Hand-set, normally 60 %. Sets TI-010.

          Upgrades you may test in Part G (BMS tab): FY-005 makes the air set point follow fuel flow (ratio); rev B adds O₂ trim from the firebox analyzer AI-028. Both are off at the start of every session.

          4 · Safety systems

          BMS sequence: IDLE → PURGING (all permissives held for the purge time) → PURGED (10 minutes to light) → RUN. Light-off needs TIC-030 in MAN with output 10–20 % and gives a 10 s trial for ignition; BS-005 must prove the flame. Any trip closes XV-301 and XV-302, opens bleed XV-303, closes FV-300, and opens FV-200 and HV-400. The first cause is latched as first out. Reset is allowed only when the cause has cleared, and a new purge is always required.

          Alarm limits

          Other protection shown on the P&ID: explosion doors (turn red if they lift after a delayed ignition), snuffing steam HV-221 to the firebox, PSV-101 on E-100.

          5 · Operating rules

          1. Air leads fuel on the way up; fuel leads air on the way down. Raise FIC-005 before you raise feed or firing.
          2. Never light without a completed purge. A failed light-off means reset and purge again, not a second try.
          3. Keep the firebox below atmospheric. PI-003 must stay negative; positive pressure pushes flue gas out of the peep doors.
          4. Read the firebox O₂ (AI-028), not only the stack O₂ (AI-029). Air leaking into the convection section makes the stack read higher than the burner sees.
          5. If fuel goes up and outlet temperature goes down, stop and think. The box may be short of air. More fuel then makes it worse.
          6. Make it safe first: reduce feed and firing to a stable point (safe-park) before you investigate.
          7. Check two instruments before you believe one: TT-040 vs TIAH-025, FI-001 vs FV-300 opening, AI-028 vs CO (AI-026).
          8. Acknowledge every alarm and say out loud what it means.

          6 · Activities

          The parts follow the course order: know the plant, walk it, understand its control and safety, read its engineering documents, operate it, train on faults, troubleshoot, then report. Times are typical for one student.

          Part A · Know the plant (about 40 min)

          1. Read the Process tab and the Design of the unit operation tab. Write the duty, the efficiency and the excess air at design, and where each comes from.
          2. Open the BFD, PFD and P&ID tabs (Process & Design group). Trace feed, fuel, air and flue gas and list every instrument on each path.
          3. On the DCS console visit Overview, Temperature profile, Draft profile and Fuel system. Sketch both profiles and mark the design values.
          4. Complete the DCS reading sheet (Exercises tab): value, low and high alarm for each tag. Graded out of 15.

          Part B · Walk the plant (about 45 min)

          Open Layout & isometrics (Engineering group) and find where each item stands, then walk the round on Visual plant 3D (Operate group). Load the Visual plant exercises from the Exercises tab (list Visual plant); each is graded out of 10.

          Part C · Control and safety (about 60 min)

          1. What-if: for each event predict ↑ / ↓ / = for all eight variables before pressing Check my predictions. Explain every wrong prediction in one sentence using a heat, mass or pressure balance.
          2. Control loop design: count the degrees of freedom and name the variable each loop controls; in the tuning lab show the offset of P-only control and how PI removes it.
          3. Safety group: from HAZOP pick one high-ranked row; follow it through Safety layers, LOPA, SRS of SIF and the C&E matrix, and write which layer acts first and how fast.

          Part D · Engineering documents (about 30 min)

          1. Project & deliverables: pick two engineering queries and say which two documents disagree in each.
          2. Process engineering and Relief & vent: check the line that fails its sizing criterion and the governing case of PSV-101; reproduce one number with the calculator.
          3. Instrumentation & control: for one trip, read its range, normal value, alarm and trip on the range bar and check its fail position against the trip action.

          Part E · Operate: cold startup (graded, limit 90 min simulated)

          Load Cold startup through the BMS from Procedures. The tracker ticks steps as you complete them:

            Part E2 · Optimisation (graded, 25 min)

            Load Optimisation: minimum safe excess air from Procedures. Trim FIC-005 in small steps until firebox O₂ (AI-028) is 1.5–2.0 % with CO below 100 ppm, TT-040 at 350 °C and FV-200 between 20 and 85 %. Record efficiency and fuel before and after, and explain what you did when conditions changed during the exercise. Compare your result with the Efficiency tab.

            Part F · Training exercises with field checks

            Load each exercise from the design state. For each one record the first alarm and its time, the first variable you noticed, what you did, and the recovery time shown in Debrief. Then go out on Visual plant 3D and do the field check listed for it: the readings and looks tick themselves from the event log and the check is graded out of 5.

            Part G · Think EQUIPPED troubleshooting with the Woods workbook

            Each case gives only a situation. Work it in the Systematic problem solving tab (Train & Assess group): pull the case, the readings against design, the trends and the event log into the workbook, and produce for each stage:

            StageWhat you must produce
            0 The problemThe symptom record with numbers and times, the operator’s trends and what normal looked like; no cause yet.
            1 EngageIs it an emergency? Decide: keep running, safe-park or shut down, and say why.
            2 DefineReference and deviation table, the two-question trigger test, IS / IS NOT, a problem statement and a measurable target.
            3 ExploreFive checks on the data, a balance that closes (or does not), the shape and order of events, symptom, cause and mechanism.
            4 PlanAt least three working hypotheses, each with a test that could refute it, ordered by safety, time and cost.
            5 Do itRun the tests with a prediction first, log the results, apply the fix safely.
            6 Look backCheck the target, name the root cause and propose a change that stops it happening again (you may test FY-005 or rev B on the BMS tab).

            Part H · Trend matching and scrambles

            In Trend matching, match four unlabelled trend sets to their events and justify each from the six pens. In Scrambles, put the steps in order; the graded result is recorded in Debrief.

            Part I · Data and report

            For your Part E run and one Part G case, download the run data CSV (Temperature profile, Draft profile, Fuel system, Controllers) at 10 s interval and the event log, and the report exported from the Woods workbook. Plot outlet temperature, fuel, air and firebox O₂ against time, and the draft profile before and after your fix.

            7 · How you are graded

            The continuous score starts at 100 and loses points every second something is wrong while the burner is firing (during a startup, shutdown or ESD procedure the temperature, O₂ and CO deductions are paused):

            DeductionRate
            TT-040 more than 1 °C from set pointup to 3 points/min, growing with the error
            Fuel-rich firebox (λ below 1)3 points/min
            Firebox O₂ too high (above 6 %)1 point/min
            CO above 400 ppm2 points/min
            Firebox pressure positive5 points/min
            Tube skin TI-024 above 430 °C / above 450 °C4 / 10 points/min
            Alarm left unacknowledged over 60 s0.3 points/min per alarm
            Unplanned BMS trip15 points each

            Procedures, the reading sheet, what-if, trend matching and scrambles are graded separately and listed under Exercise grades in the Debrief tab, together with fault recovery times.

            Visual plant exercises (VP-1 to VP-8, out of 10), field checks of the training exercises (out of 5), the identification and the rounds sheet are listed there too.

            8 · Report checklist

            • Part A notes and sketches, reading-sheet score.
            • Part B Visual plant grades (VP-1 to VP-4, identification, rounds sheet).
            • Part C what-if table with corrections; one HAZOP row followed to its SIF.
            • Part D two engineering queries, one PSV and one instrument checked.
            • Part E procedure grades, time to line out, and trend plots.
            • Part F table for every training exercise with its field-check grade; VP-5 and VP-6.
            • Part G downloaded six-stage workbook for each assigned case, with evidence from the console and CSV plots.
            • Debrief screenshot: continuous score, deductions and exercise grades.
            • One recommended control improvement, with before/after data.

            5 · Differences from rev C (the reference drawing above)

            • PT-020 / PIAL-020 / PSLL-020 drawn at the gun, downstream of FV-300, where the process description puts the 600 kPa atomising pressure; PI-019 is drawn on the fuel header (about 1940 kPa) upstream of the shut-off valves. Rev C shows them the other way round; the simulator values are the same.
            • Pump suction and discharge block valves and check valves, FV-010 block-and-bypass, E-100 channel drain, coil high-point vent and outlet low-point drain added.
            • Field transmitters shown separately from the DCS and SIS functions (FT-008, FT-005, TE-025, PT-030, PT-020), so shared-sensor issues such as FT-008 are visible.
